# 3. Payload Setting

**Goal:** Register the **mass** and **center of mass (X/Y/Z)** of the add-on module in the RBQ app so the robot accounts for it while walking.

**Prerequisites:** Step 2, [Rail & Spring Nut](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/add-on/rail-spring-nut.html), must be complete — the module has to be physically mounted on the rail.

## Before you start

- Put the robot on **flat, stable ground**.
- The RBQ app must be **connected** to the robot ([Controller & Wi-Fi](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/controller-wifi-connect.html) complete).
- Measure the module's center of mass as **X / Y / Z (m)** relative to the center of the robot body.

## Procedure

1. Open **Robot settings › Payload setup** in the app. The `Payload Configuration` screen appears.

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/settings-robot.pc.en.png' alt='Robot parameters — Payload Configuration' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Robot settings › Payload setup</figcaption>
</figure>

2. In the **slot table** on the right, tap the slot you want and **tick its checkbox.** Ticking it fills in the catalogue defaults the robot holds.
3. Enter the values in the **editor** on the left:
   - **Mass (kg)** — mass of the add-on module
   - **X / Y / Z (m)** — center of mass in the robot coordinate frame

   Tap a field to type, or use `−` and `+`; the **Interval** chips (`0.001`, `0.01`, `0.1`, `1`) set how much each press moves the value.
4. Check the **total** below the editor for the combined mass and center of mass. Going over the limit turns it red and blocks sending.
5. Press **Set Payload** and confirm with **Apply**. Unticked slots are sent with mass 0, which clears them.
6. After applying, press **Get** to re-read the stored values and confirm them.

## Buttons

| Button | Function |
|---|---|
| **Checkbox** | Marks the slot as mounted (unticking sends mass 0, clearing it) |
| **Interval** | How much `−` and `+` move the value (`0.001`, `0.01`, `0.1`, `1`) |
| **Set Payload** | Applies every edited slot to the robot, via a confirmation |
| **Get** | Re-reads the values stored on the robot — edits in progress are discarded |

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>Registering the payload is not enough on its own — the next step, ZMP calibration, adjusts the posture so the robot balances under the new load.</p>
</div>
</div>

Allowed ranges and error messages are listed on [Payload configuration](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/troubleshooting/payload_setting.html).

## Next step

With the payload registered, run the ZMP calibration to rebalance under the new weight:

**[→ 4. ZMP Calibration](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/add-on/zmp-calibration.html)**

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/add-on/rail-spring-nut.html
================================================================================

# 2. Rail & Spring Nut

**Goal:** Mount your add-on hardware to the robot's top rail using spring nuts.

**Prerequisites:** Step 1 [Specifications Check](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/add-on/specifications.html) is complete — the add-on is within payload and interface limits.


## What You Need

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Spring nuts** | MISUMI **SHNTP5-5** ([KR](https://kr.misumi-ec.com/vona2/detail/110302608410/?HissuCode=SHNTP5-5&PNSearch=SHNTP5-5&searchFlow=results2products&list=PageSearchResult) · [US](https://us.misumi-ec.com/vona2/detail/110302247640/?PNSearch=SHNTP5-5&HissuCode=SHNTP5-5&seriesCode=110302247640&tab=drawingAndSpecifications&Page=1)) |
| **Bolts** | M5 bolts that match your add-on's mounting holes |
| **Rigid rod** | **≤ 4 mm diameter**, for removal |

The robot top uses rails for mounting optional hardware (PTZ cameras, LiDAR, custom brackets). Spring nuts inserted into the rail slot give you threaded anchor points for M5 bolts.

## Insert a Spring Nut

1. **Insert at an angle** — slide the spring nut **diagonally** into the rail slot so it enters the internal channel.
2. **Press the protruding section** — a portion of the nut may sit proud of the slot; press it down so the nut seats fully.
3. **Align with the rail** — adjust the nut so it is aligned with the slot and can slide freely along the rail.

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/insert-1.png' alt='Step 1 - diagonal insert' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 1 — diagonal insert</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/insert-2.png' alt='Step 2 - press the protruding section' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 2 — press the protruding section</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/insert-3.png' alt='Step 3 - align with the slot' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 3 — align with the slot</figcaption>
</figure>

Slide the nut to the position where your add-on bracket should sit, then tighten the M5 bolt to fix the bracket.

## Remove a Spring Nut

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p><strong>Tool diameter:</strong> use a rigid rod <strong>no larger than 4 mm</strong> in diameter. A thicker tool can damage the nut or mar the rail slot.</p>
</div>
</div>

1. **Insert a rod** — pass a rigid rod (**≤ 4 mm**) through the hole in the spring nut.
2. **Push against one wall** — push the nut against one inner wall of the rail slot.
3. **Twist and lift** — while holding it against that wall, twist and lift toward the opposite side so the nut clears the rail profile.
4. **Remove** — withdraw the nut from the slot.

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/remove-1.png' alt='Step 1 - rod through the hole' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 1 — rod through the hole</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/remove-2.png' alt='Step 2 - push to one wall' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 2 — push to one wall</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/remove-3.png' alt='Step 3 - twist and lift' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 3 — twist and lift</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/remove-4.png' alt='Step 4 - remove' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 4 — remove</figcaption>
</figure>

## Next Step

Hardware is mounted. Now register the add-on's mass and offset in the GUI:

**[→ 3. Payload Setting](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/add-on/payload-setting.html)**

SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/add-on/specifications.html

# 1. Specifications Check

**Goal:** Verify your add-on (camera, LiDAR, computer, sensor, etc.) is within the robot's mechanical and electrical limits **before** attaching it.

**Prerequisites:** None. Run this check first whenever you plan to install a new module.


## Key Limits for RBQ 10

| Parameter | Limit | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Max Payload** | **15 kg** | Total mass of everything mounted on top of the robot |
| **Mounting interface** | **Top rail (slot)** + spring nuts | Use rail slots for repeatable, secure mounting |
| **Power available** | **54 V**, **12 V** | Check your add-on's input voltage / current draw |
| **Data interfaces** | **CAN ×1**, **Gigabit LAN ×3** | Match your add-on's communication interface |
| **Ingress Protection** | **IP54** | Add-ons should not compromise IP rating in field use |

For the full specification table (dimensions, walking speed, slope, sensors, etc.), see the manual page below.

**[→ Full Specifications (manual)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/product-descriptions/general-specification.html)**

## Pre-installation Checklist

Before moving to the next step, confirm:

- [ ] Add-on mass + any existing payload **≤ 15 kg**
- [ ] Center of mass is **roughly above the robot body** (avoid large overhang)
- [ ] Power and data interfaces match what RBQ 10 provides
- [ ] You have **measured the X / Y / Z offset** of the add-on's center of mass from the robot body center (needed in step 3)

<div class="sb sb-warning">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">WARNING</p>
<p>Exceeding the <strong>15 kg</strong> payload limit or mounting mass far from the body center can destabilize walking, increase joint load, and shorten component life. Always check the spec sheet first.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Next Step

When your add-on passes the checklist, mount it to the rail:

**[→ 2. Rail & Spring Nut](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/add-on/rail-spring-nut.html)**

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/add-on/zmp-calibration.html
================================================================================

# 4. ZMP Calibration

**Goal:** Recalibrate the Zero Moment Point so the robot stays balanced under the weight the add-on module has changed.

**Prerequisites:** Step 3, [Payload Setting](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/add-on/payload-setting.html), must be complete — the mass and center of mass have to be registered on the robot.

## What ZMP calibration does

ZMP (Zero Moment Point) calibration aligns the center of the ground reaction force while the robot stands, so it stays balanced as it walks. A changed payload moves the center of mass, which is why this step is needed.

## Before you start

- Put the robot on **flat, firm ground**.
- Clear the area so **nothing and nobody touches the robot**, and leave **room for one step**.
- The app must be connected and **the robot must be standing** (STAND). It cannot start while sitting.

## Procedure

1. Open **Robot settings → Calibration** in the app.

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/settings-cal.pc.en.png" alt="Robot settings → Calibration" style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 1 — Robot settings → Calibration</figcaption>
</figure>

2. Under **ZMP Calibration**, press `Auto-calibrate ZMP offset`. If the robot cannot run it, the button is locked and the reason appears right there.
3. Confirm in the dialog.
4. The robot **takes one step to square up its legs**, then calibrates — **up to 60 seconds**.
5. When it is done the robot **saves the value itself and returns to STAND.**
6. Switch Stance → Walk and confirm the robot walks normally with the module fitted.

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Do not put anything on the robot or push it during calibration. A failure leaves the previous calibration in place; what to do for each reason is listed in <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/troubleshooting/calibration-tuning.html">Calibration and tuning</a>.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Done

The add-on module is fitted, the payload is registered and the ZMP is calibrated. You can send motion commands as usual — see **[Motion commands](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/motion-commands.html)** for driving the robot.

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/charging.html
================================================================================

# 3. Charging

**Goal:** Safely charge the RBQ10 battery after use.

The RBQ10 supports three charging methods:
- **Charger** — connect directly to the charging port on the top of the robot
- **Docking station** — autonomous docking and charging via the bottom port
- **External cable from docking station** — connect the station's cable to the robot's top port manually

**Prerequisites:** The robot must be powered off before connecting any charging cable.

<div class="sb sb-warning">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">WARNING</p>
<p>Charge the robot only with the supplied RBQ10 charger or RBQ10 docking station.</p>
</div>
</div>

  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ Charge robot with external cable ]</figcaption>
</figure>

## Docking station installation precautions

1. The charging station is water-resistant, but if water is present on the charging terminals, charging problems may occur; install it away from places where water splashes.
2. The power cable is treated for water exposure, but when connecting to an external outlet, keep water out of the plug connection.
3. Prolonged direct sunlight can cause overheating; installing in a shaded location is recommended.
4. Secure the charging station to the floor using the fixing holes.

## Next Step

When the robot is fully charged, pack it for storage or transport:

**[→ 4. Packing](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/packing.html)**

# 2. Controller & Wi-Fi Connection

**Goal:** Connect the controller to the robot Wi-Fi, then connect the RBQ app to the robot and complete the automatic start so the robot is ready to operate.

**Prerequisites:** [Initial Pose & Power On](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/initial-pose.html) must be completed first — the robot must be on and initialized.

## Step 1: Wi-Fi connection

The robot provides a Wi-Fi access point named `RBQ_{XX}` (XX differs by unit). Connect the controller (Steam Deck, tablet or PC) to that network.

The app opens on the **hub**, and the status line after the robot name says whether the device is on the right network.

<figure style="text-align: center; margin: 0.5rem auto 1.25rem;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/hub.pc.en.png' alt='The hub — robot name and status line' style="display: block; width: 100%; max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 0 auto; border-radius: 6px; box-shadow: 0 1px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.07);" />
  <figcaption style="margin-top: 0.5rem; text-align: center; color: var(--vp-c-text-2, #666); font-size: 0.95em;">[ The hub ]</figcaption>
</figure>

1. **Read the status line** - `Connect to the robot's WiFi` means no robot is saved yet; `Not on the robot's WiFi` means the device is on another network, and the app names the robot's WiFi when it knows it.
2. **Select the robot network** - On Linux desktop and Steam Deck, `Switch WiFi` next to the line joins that network or opens the in-app list so you can pick `RBQ_{XX}`. Android offers `WiFi settings`; on iOS and the web build, join from the device's own Wi-Fi settings. (If it does not appear, check robot power and Wi-Fi operation.)
3. **Confirm** - You are ready once the dot in front of the robot name turns green.

The full procedure is in [Controller and Wi-Fi](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/operation/controller-wifi-connect.html#wifi).

## Step 2: Connect the app to the robot {#connect}

Open the RBQ app and connect it to the robot. The procedure — entering the robot address, connecting and checking the link status — is described in **[Connection](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/connection.html)**.

## Step 3: Auto start {#auto-start}

Bring up the robot software and state with the automatic start sequence from the control screen. See **[Control home](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/control-home.html)** for the sequence and how to confirm that every item has completed. If an item fails, keep people away from the robot, review the [emergency stop procedures](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/emergency-stop-procedures.html), and follow the [general safety guidelines](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/general-safety-warning-precautions.html). If the problem persists, contact Rainbow Robotics via [error reporting](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/support/).

## Next Step

The robot is connected and ready to drive. The app's screens and buttons are covered in **[the RBQ app](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/introduction.html)**, **[Control home](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/control-home.html)** and **[Motion commands](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/motion-commands.html)**.

What to do once you are finished operating:

**[→ 3. Charging](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/charging.html)**

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/emo.html
================================================================================

# 5. Emergency Stop & Recovery

**Goal:** Know how to stop the robot immediately in an emergency and how to safely resume operation.

<div class="sb sb-warning">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">WARNING</p>
<p>Always keep the emergency stop button accessible during operation. In any situation where the robot poses a risk to people or property, press the emergency stop button immediately.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Physical Emergency Stop Button

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/emo.png' alt='Emergency stop button on the rear of the robot' />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ Emergency stop push button — located on the rear of the robot ]</figcaption>
</figure>

When the **emergency stop button** is pressed:

- All joints switch to **High Damping** mode.
- The robot resists external motion but does **not** accept torque or position commands.
- The robot may lose its posture and settle to the ground under gravity.

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>High Damping mode protects both the user and the robot. The robot will not execute any motion commands until the emergency stop is cleared and the robot is re-initialized.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Emergency stop from the app

The RBQ app has an `E-STOP` button at the right of the top bar on the control home, and in the same place on the other screens while a robot is connected — if the link drops it stays live for 8 seconds. It asks for confirmation and then has the same effect as the physical button — all joints enter High Damping mode. See **[Emergency Stop](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/emergency.html)** for the confirmation dialog and what happens when another device takes control; the forced-recovery tools are on **[Developer mode](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/developer-mode.html#emergency)**.

## Recovery Procedure

After an emergency stop, follow these steps to safely resume operation:

1. **Ensure safety** — Confirm that all people and animals have moved at least 2 m away from the robot.
2. **Release the button** — Rotate the physical emergency stop button clockwise to return it to its original (unlocked) position.
3. **Return to initial pose** — If the robot has fallen or shifted, manually return it to the [correct initial pose](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/initial-pose.html) on a flat surface.
4. **Re-initialize** — Run the automatic start sequence or the Stand motion from the [control home](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/control-home.html).
5. **Verify** — Confirm that the robot state in the top bar is normal and that every start item has completed before resuming operation.

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Do not attempt to force-move the joints while the robot is in High Damping mode. Return the robot to the initial pose carefully and only after the emergency stop has been released.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Related

- [General Safety Guidelines](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/general-safety-warning-precautions.html)
- [Emergency Stop Procedures (detailed)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/emergency-stop-procedures.html)
- [Initial Pose & Power On](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/initial-pose.html)

# 1. Initial Pose & Power On

**Goal:** Place the robot in the correct initial pose on a flat surface, then power it on.

<div class="sb sb-required">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-book" aria-hidden="true">📖</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">REQUIRED READING</p>
<p>Before operating the robot, read the <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/general-safety-warning-precautions.html">General Safety Guidelines</a> and the <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/indications.html">Safety Indications</a>.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Prerequisites

- A flat, stable floor with sufficient open space (minimum 2 m radius clearance around the robot)
- The robot battery is charged
- No people or animals within 2 m of the robot

## Setting the Initial Pose

Place the robot on the floor so that all feet and knees contact the ground simultaneously.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/initial-pose-1.png' alt='RBQ10 correct initial pose overview' />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ RBQ10 Initial Pose ]</figcaption>
</figure>

### Step 1. Choose a flat surface

Place the robot on a level floor. Uneven surfaces can cause Auto Start to fail.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/initial-pose-2.png' alt='Flat surface requirement' />
</figure>

### Step 2. Fully fold the knee joints

Fold all four knee joints completely so the knee pads are close to the ground.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/initial-pose-3.png' alt='Fold knee joints' />
</figure>

### Step 3. Set all three ground contact points

Rotate the hip pitch and roll joints until **three points per leg** contact the floor: the **body bumper**, the **knee joint**, and the **foot**.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/initial-pose-4.png' alt='Three ground contact points' />
</figure>

<div class="sb sb-warning">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">WARNING</p>
<p>If the initial pose is incorrect, Auto Start will fail and the robot may fall unexpectedly. Always confirm all contact points before powering on.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Power On

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/power-button.png" alt="Power button" style="width: 300px;" />
</figure>

1. Press the **Power Button** on the robot body.
2. Confirm the **red indicator** light on the button turns on.
3. Listen for the **double-beep** sound — this confirms the boot sequence has started.

The robot will take about 30–60 seconds to fully initialize. Do not attempt to move the robot during this time.

## Next Step

Once the robot is on and initialized, proceed to connect the controller and Wi-Fi:

**[→ 2. Controller & Wi-Fi Connection](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/controller-wifi-connect.html)**

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/packing.html
================================================================================

# 4. Packing

**Goal:** Safely pack the RBQ10 into its Pelican case for storage or transport.

**Prerequisites:** The robot is powered off and all additional attached equipment has been removed.

The RBQ10 is stored and transported using a **Pelican 1730 Protector Case**. The model of the Pelican case used is the 1730 Protector Case. Please refer to the images below and store the RBQ10 along with other items accordingly.


## Robot packing and unpacking
The Pelican case has two layers. The lower layer holds the charger, spare rubber feet, and LiDAR; the RBQ10 is placed on top of them.
<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-1.png' alt='Pelican case lower layer layout' />
</figure>

After arranging items in the lower layer, carry the robot as shown in the figure and place it in the case.

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>The robot must be carried by two people working together.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Before transporting the robot, remove any additional equipment attached to it and turn off the power.</p>
</div>
</div>

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-2.png' alt='Carrying robot into case' />
</figure>

After setting the RBQ10 on the floor, extend the legs as shown in the figure.

Two people should carry the robot, each holding one of the leg areas marked in red.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-3.png' alt='Transport with legs extended' />
</figure>

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Be careful not to let any foreign objects get into the knee joint rotation area, and ensure fingers do not get pinched!</p>
</div>
</div>

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-4.png' alt='Knee joint caution pose' />
</figure>

Place the robot in the Pelican 1730 case to match the case shape.

After the body is in the case, fold the legs in this order:

### Step 1: Fold the front legs’ knee joints fully
<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-5.png' alt='Front leg knee fold step 1' />
</figure>

### Step 2: Rotate the front legs’ hip pitch joints and place the legs into the case recesses

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-6.png' alt='Front leg hip pitch rotation step 2' />
</figure>
<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-7.png' alt='Front leg placed in case step 2 (continued)' />
</figure>

### Step 3: Rotate the rear legs’ hip pitch joints so the legs go over the front thighs

### Step 4: Fully extend the rear shins
<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-8.png' alt='Rear leg shin extension step 4' />
</figure>

Place the remote controller in the side storage next to the robot. Remaining empty space can be used as needed.

Close the lid to finish packing.

Unpacking is the reverse of the above steps.

# Developer Setup Guide

**Goal:** Clone the RBQ repository, set up the development environment, and launch the simulator so you can test robot behavior before running on hardware.

<div class="sb sb-required">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-book" aria-hidden="true">📖</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">REQUIRED READING</p>
<p>Familiarize yourself with the safety guidelines before testing on the real robot: <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/general-safety-warning-precautions.html">General Safety Guidelines</a>.</p>
</div>
</div>

## System Requirements

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| OS | Ubuntu 22.04 (x86-64) |
| CPU | Intel Core i7 12th Gen or equivalent |
| RAM | 16 GB or more |
| Storage | 25 GB free space |
| Control | Keyboard (W/A/S/D, Q/E, arrow keys) or Logitech F710 gamepad |

## Step 1. Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/RainbowRobotics/RBQ.git
cd RBQ
```

> All SDK source code, examples, scripts, and simulator environments live inside `RBQ/`.  
> Run all commands from this directory unless stated otherwise.

> **Note:** Pre-built binaries ship in `bin-x86_64/` (and `bin-aarch64/` for arm64). No compilation step is required to run the simulator or deploy to the robot.

## Step 2. Launch the Simulator

The simulator runs in Docker — Docker is the only thing to install, and the script offers to install it when it is missing. The first run takes a few minutes to build its image. See [MuJoCo](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/simulator/mujoco.html).

Start the RBQ control stack and the MuJoCo physics simulator together:

```bash
bash scripts/sim.bash --no-gui          # motion only
bash scripts/sim.bash --no-gui --vision # motion + vision sensors
```

It runs in the foreground of this terminal; Ctrl-C stops it. If Docker needs `sudo` on this PC, enter your password when asked.

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>Pass <code>--no-gui</code>. This repository carries no on-PC control GUI — you drive the simulator from the <strong>RBQ</strong> app, exactly as you drive the real robot.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Step 3. Connect and stand the robot up in the RBQ app

Install the RBQ desktop app from the **[Downloads](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/downloads/)** page, then:

1. Start the app **on the same PC** as the simulator. With no robot network around, the desktop app finds the MuJoCo simulator on this PC by itself and connects — see [Connection](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/connection.html).
2. Press **Control** on the hub to open the control home.
3. Tap the green **Auto Start** pill, press **Auto Start** in the dialog, and wait for the sequence to report **Done**. Press **Close**.
4. Press `STAND` on the motion card to stand the robot up.

The robot is now ready to receive commands. Refer to [Motion commands](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/motion-commands.html) for joystick and gait control.

## Step 4. Run on the Real Robot

When you are ready to test on hardware:

1. Place the robot in the [correct initial pose](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/common/initial-pose.html).
2. Connect your device to the robot Wi-Fi (`RBQ_xxxx`).
3. Open the RBQ app and pick the robot in the robot list — see [Connection](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/connection.html).
4. Press **Control**, run **Auto Start**, then press `STAND`.

The steps are the same ones you just used against the simulator, which is the point of rehearsing there first.

> It is strongly recommended to verify all behaviors in simulation before testing on the real robot.

## Step 5. Update the Robot

Robot software is updated from the app with **`Send robot software`** on the `Software update`
screen. The robot deploys it as soon as the transfer completes, and the app then offers a reboot.

**→ [Robot Software Update](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/software-update.html)**

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Put the robot in the <strong>sitting</strong> state before restarting, and do not move it until the restart finishes. Running a mismatched binary and script combination can cause unexpected behavior.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Detailed Reference

| Topic | Link |
|---|---|
| Full walkthrough | [Developers Guide (Software)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/developers-guide.html) |
| The RBQ app, screen by screen | [RBQ App](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/introduction.html) |
| Simulation environment | [MuJoCo Simulation](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/developers-guide.html#simulation) |
| Concepts & architecture | [Concept](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/concept.html) |

# High Level Command — Quick Start

**Source**: `rbq_sdk/cpp/example/src/rbq_high_level.cpp`

Publishes `HighLevelCommand` at 50 Hz. Type gait names in the terminal; control velocity with a joystick.

## Build

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/cpp/example
bash scripts/setup.bash
bash scripts/build.bash
```

## Run

```bash
./bin/rbq_high_level [networkInterface] [joystickPath]

# Simulator / on-robot stack — interface defaults to lo
./bin/rbq_high_level

# Real robot — pass the interface that reaches it
./bin/rbq_high_level eth0
```

A joystick is required. The program auto-detects `/dev/input/js*` (prefers Logitech/Xbox by name).  
Override with an explicit path: `./bin/rbq_high_level eth0 /dev/input/js1`

## Terminal usage

```
list              ← print the example's built-in list
standing          ← switch by name
3                 ← switch by ID (trotting)
waving            ← switch to wave gait
```

## Supported gaits

| Name | ID | Notes |
|------|----|-------|
| `sitting` | 0 | Sit down |
| `standing` | 1 | Default at startup |
| `trotting` | 3 | MPC trot |
| `trot_stairs` | 4 | Stair-climbing trot |
| `waving` | 5 | Wave gait |
| `docking` | 10 | Auto-docking sequence |

> The example's built-in list also prints internal gaits that are not supported. Use only the gaits in the table above.

After commanding `docking` (10), monitor the sequence via the `docking_state` field of
`RobotStatus` — it reports each stage and, on abort, the failure reason. See the
[docking-state table](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/ros/topics.html#robot-status).

## Joystick velocity

| Axis | Command | Max |
|------|---------|-----|
| L stick forward/back | `vel_x` | ±1.2 m/s |
| L stick left/right | `vel_y` | ±0.5 m/s |
| R stick left/right | `omega_z` | ±60 deg/s |

> `omega_z` is in **deg/s** — QuadWalk converts to rad/s internally.

## Important

The program sends `switchControlMode = true` at startup.  
Without this, the robot ignores `HighLevelCommand` and stays in joystick mode.

→ **Full reference**: [High Level Command](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/cpp/high-level.html)

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/low-level.html
================================================================================

# Low Level (RL Policy) — Quick Start

**Source**: `rbq_sdk/cpp/example/src/rbq_low_level.cpp`

Runs a learned walking policy (ONNX) on the robot at 100 Hz via low-level joint control.

## Build

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/cpp/example
bash scripts/setup.bash
bash scripts/build.bash
```

## Run

From `RBQ/rbq_sdk/cpp/example/`:

```bash
# Use sudo for real-time thread; without sudo = normal thread
sudo ./bin/rbq_low_level -p <policyDir> [networkInterface]

# Simulator / on-robot stack — interface defaults to lo
sudo ./bin/rbq_low_level -p ../../../rbq_simulator/rbq_gym/policy/rbq10/

# Real robot — pass the interface that reaches it
sudo ./bin/rbq_low_level -p ../../../rbq_simulator/rbq_gym/policy/rbq10/ eth0
```

`-p` is **required** — pass a directory containing `info.json` and `policy.onnx`.  
`networkInterface` is optional and defaults to `lo`.

## Run with simulation

1. From `RBQ/` root, start the simulator:
   ```bash
   bash scripts/sim.bash --no-gui
   ```
2. In the **RBQ** app on the same PC — started there, the desktop app finds this simulator on its own: **Control** → **Auto Start** → `STAND`. See [Control home](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/control-home.html).
3. Run the example:
   ```bash
   sudo ./bin/rbq_low_level -p ../../../rbq_simulator/rbq_gym/policy/rbq10/
   ```

## Keyboard controls

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `x` | Stand up (ready posture) |
| `z` | Sit down (ground posture) |
| `c` | Start walking (loads policy) |
| `q` | Quit |

## Policy directory

Pre-trained policies are in the repository at:
```
rbq_simulator/rbq_gym/policy/rbq10/
├── info.json
└── policy.onnx
```

Trained your own policy with [Isaac Gym](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/simulator/rbq-gym.html) or [Isaac Lab](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/simulator/rbq-lab.html)?  
Point `-p` at the exported directory (`policy.onnx` + `info.json`).

## State machine

| State | How to enter | What happens |
|-------|-------------|-------------|
| Idle | (default) | Mirrors the stack's final reference |
| Motion | `x` or `z` | Interpolates to ready / ground posture |
| Control | `c` | Runs ONNX policy at 100 Hz, publishes joint references |

→ **Full reference**: [Low Level (RL Policy)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/cpp/low-level.html)

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/quick-start.html
================================================================================

# RBQ C++ SDK — Quick Start

Get the SDK built and your first example running in 5 steps.

## 1. Clone the repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/RainbowRobotics/RBQ.git
cd RBQ
```

> All scripts, SDK source code, and examples are in the repository root. Run all commands from `RBQ/` unless stated otherwise.

## 2. Build the C++ SDK

```bash
cd rbq_sdk/cpp/rbq_sdk_cpp

# First time only — build bundled CycloneDDS
sudo bash scripts/build_dds.bash

# Build and install the SDK
sudo bash scripts/build.bash

cd ../../..
```

## 3. Build the examples

```bash
cd rbq_sdk/cpp/example

# Install build dependencies (first time only)
bash scripts/setup.bash

# Build examples
bash scripts/build.bash

cd ../../..
```

Binaries are placed in `rbq_sdk/cpp/example/bin/`.

## 4. Start the simulator (skip for real hardware)

The simulator runs in Docker — Docker is the only thing to install, and the script offers to install it when it is missing. The first run takes a few minutes to build its image. See [MuJoCo](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/simulator/mujoco.html).

From the `RBQ/` root:

```bash
bash scripts/sim.bash --no-gui
```

Start the **RBQ** app on the same PC — the desktop app finds this simulator on its own:
1. **Control** on the hub → the control home opens.
2. **Auto Start** → press **Auto Start** in the dialog and wait for **Done**, then **Close**.
3. `STAND` on the motion card → the robot stands up.

See [Control home](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/control-home.html) for the full screen.

## 5. Run your first example

From `rbq_sdk/cpp/example/`:

```bash
# Terminal-based command test
./bin/rbq_sport_client

# Joystick control
./bin/rbq_sport_client_joy

# High-level gait + velocity (requires joystick)
./bin/rbq_high_level

# Low-level RL policy
sudo ./bin/rbq_low_level -p ../../../rbq_simulator/rbq_gym/policy/rbq10/
```

Every example defaults to the loopback interface (`lo`) — the same one the
simulator and the on-robot stack use — so no argument is needed while the whole
stack runs on this PC.

**On a real robot**, pass the interface that reaches it as the first argument:

```bash
./bin/rbq_sport_client eth0
```

Check your interface name with `ip link`.  
For robot Wi-Fi (`RBQ_xxxx`), use the Wi-Fi interface (e.g. `wlp4s0`).

## Examples overview

| Example | Binary | What it does |
|---------|--------|-------------|
| [Sport Client →](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/sport-client.html) | `rbq_sport_client` | Terminal CLI — test any SportClient command |
| [Sport Client (Joy) →](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/sport-client-joy.html) | `rbq_sport_client_joy` | Gamepad — full button mapping |
| [High Level Cmd →](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/high-level.html) | `rbq_high_level` | 50 Hz gait + joystick velocity |
| [Low Level (Policy) →](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/low-level.html) | `rbq_low_level` | Joint control + ONNX RL policy |

→ **Build issues?** See [SDK Build Issues](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/troubleshooting/sdk-build.html)

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/sport-client-joy.html
================================================================================

# Sport Client (Joystick) — Quick Start

**Source**: `rbq_sdk/cpp/example/src/rbq_sport_client_joy.cpp`

Gamepad-driven robot control via SportClient. Analog sticks → velocity, buttons → discrete actions.

## Build

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/cpp/example
bash scripts/setup.bash
bash scripts/build.bash
```

## Run

```bash
./bin/rbq_sport_client_joy [networkInterface] [joystickPath]

# Simulator / on-robot stack — interface defaults to lo
./bin/rbq_sport_client_joy

# Real robot — pass the interface that reaches it
./bin/rbq_sport_client_joy eth0
./bin/rbq_sport_client_joy eth0 /dev/input/js1
```

Joystick is auto-detected from `/dev/input/js*` (prefers Logitech/Xbox by name).  
Override with `JOY=/dev/input/js1 ./bin/rbq_sport_client_joy eth0`.

## Gamepad layout (Logitech F710 / Xbox)

### Button chords

| Hold + Press | Action |
|-------------|--------|
| **L2 + B** | E-stop (Damp) |
| **L2 + A** × 1 | StandUp (lock joints) |
| **L2 + A** × 2 | StandDown (prone) |
| **START** | Default gait |
| **L2 + START** | Running mode |
| **L2 + X** | Recovery stand |
| **R1 + X** | Climb mode |
| **BACK** | Stop move |

### Double-click (within 400 ms)

| Button | Action |
|--------|--------|
| X × 2 | Left-side gait |
| Y × 2 | Right-side gait |

### Analog sticks

| Axis | Maps to | Max |
|------|---------|-----|
| L stick forward/back | vel_x | ±0.55 m/s |
| L stick left/right | vel_y | ±0.35 m/s |
| R stick left/right | vyaw | ±1.0 rad/s |

Deadzone: 0.12 on all axes.

→ **Full reference**: [Sport Client (Joystick)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/cpp/sport-client-joy.html)

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/sport-client.html
================================================================================

# Sport Client — Quick Start

**Source**: `rbq_sdk/cpp/example/src/rbq_sport_client.cpp`

Interactive terminal CLI that sends any SportClient command to the robot.

## Build

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/cpp/example
bash scripts/setup.bash
bash scripts/build.bash
```

## Run

```bash
./bin/rbq_sport_client [networkInterface]

# Simulator / on-robot stack — interface defaults to lo
./bin/rbq_sport_client

# Real robot — pass the interface that reaches it
./bin/rbq_sport_client eth0
```

## Usage

```
Input "list " to list all test option ...
list              ← print all commands
balance_stand     ← execute by name
1                 ← execute by ID
```

## Commands

| ID | Name | What it does |
|----|------|-------------|
| 0 | `damp` | High-damping e-stop |
| 1 | `balance_stand` | Balanced standing |
| 2 | `stop_move` | Stop in place |
| 3 | `stand_down` | Go prone |
| 4 | `recovery_stand` | Stand up from fall |
| 5 | `move` | Rotate in place (`Move(0, 0, 0.5)`) |
| 6 | `switch_gait` | Switch to default gait |
| 8 | `get_state` | Print FSM state / speed level / process state |
| 11 | `stand_up` | Lock joints in standing position |

> The example program's `list` also prints commands the robot does not implement; those return a
> "not implemented" error. Only the commands above are supported.

> Full list: type `list` at the prompt. Unknown commands print a guidance message.

## Notes

- The client uses `SetNoReply(true)` — fire-and-forget, no RPC wait.
- Loop runs at 50 Hz; the selected command executes on every tick.

→ **Full reference**: [Sport Client (Software)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/cpp/sport-client.html)

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-python/high-level.html
================================================================================

# High Level Command (Python) — Quick Start

**Source**: `rbq_sdk/python/example/sport/rbq_high_level.py`

Python port of the C++ `rbq_high_level` example. Publishes `HighLevelCommand` at 50 Hz, selects gaits via terminal, and controls velocity with a joystick.

## Install

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/python
pip install -e .
```

## Run

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/python/example/sport
python3 rbq_high_level.py [networkInterface] [joystickPath]

# Simulator / on-robot stack — interface defaults to lo
python3 rbq_high_level.py

# Real robot — pass the interface that reaches it
python3 rbq_high_level.py eth0
```

A joystick is required. The program auto-detects `/dev/input/js*` (prefers Logitech/Xbox by name).  
Override via argument or `JOY=/dev/input/js1 python3 rbq_high_level.py eth0`.

## Terminal usage

```
list              ← print the example's built-in list
standing          ← switch by name
3                 ← switch by ID (trotting)
waving            ← switch to wave gait
```

## Supported gaits

| Name | ID | Notes |
|------|----|-------|
| `sitting` | 0 | Sit down |
| `standing` | 1 | Default at startup |
| `trotting` | 3 | MPC trot |
| `trot_stairs` | 4 | Stair-climbing trot |
| `waving` | 5 | Wave gait |
| `docking` | 10 | Auto-docking sequence |

> The example's built-in list also prints internal gaits that are not supported. Use only the gaits in the table above.

After commanding `docking` (10), monitor the sequence via the `docking_state` field of
`RobotStatus` — it reports each stage and, on abort, the failure reason. See the
[docking-state table](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/ros/topics.html#robot-status).

## Joystick velocity

| Axis | Command | Max |
|------|---------|-----|
| L stick forward/back | `vel_x` | ±1.2 m/s |
| L stick left/right | `vel_y` | ±0.5 m/s |
| R stick left/right | `omega_z` | ±60 deg/s |

> `omega_z` is in **deg/s** — QuadWalk converts to rad/s internally.

## Important

The program sends `switchControlMode = true` at startup.  
Without this, the robot ignores `HighLevelCommand` and stays in joystick mode.

→ **C++ version**: [High Level Command (C++)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/high-level.html)

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-python/low-level.html
================================================================================

# Low Level (RL Policy) Python — Quick Start

**Source**: `rbq_sdk/python/example/sport/rbq_low_level.py`

Python port of the C++ `rbq_low_level` example. Loads an RL policy (`info.json` + `policy.onnx`) and drives leg joints via low-level joint control at 100 Hz.

## Install

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/python
pip install -e .
pip install onnxruntime
```

## Run

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/python/example/sport
python3 rbq_low_level.py -p <policyDir> [networkInterface]
```

```bash
# Simulator / on-robot stack — interface defaults to lo
python3 rbq_low_level.py -p ../../../../rbq_simulator/rbq_gym/policy/rbq10/

# Real robot
python3 rbq_low_level.py -p ../../../../rbq_simulator/rbq_gym/policy/rbq10/ eth0
```

`-p` is **required** — pass a directory containing `info.json` and `policy.onnx`.

> Unlike the C++ version, no `sudo` is needed (Python does not use a real-time thread).

## Run with simulation

1. From `RBQ/` root, start the simulator:
   ```bash
   bash scripts/sim.bash --no-gui
   ```
2. In the **RBQ** app on the same PC — started there, the desktop app finds this simulator on its own: **Control** → **Auto Start** → `STAND`. See [Control home](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/control-home.html).
3. Run the example (interface defaults to `lo`):
   ```bash
   python3 rbq_low_level.py -p ../../../../rbq_simulator/rbq_gym/policy/rbq10/
   ```

## Keyboard controls

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `x` | Stand up (ready posture) |
| `z` | Sit down (ground posture) |
| `c` | Start walking (loads and runs policy) |
| `q` | Quit |

## Policy directory

Pre-trained policies are included in the repository:

```
rbq_simulator/rbq_gym/policy/rbq10/
├── info.json
└── policy.onnx
```

Supported policy names (from `info.json`): `rbq10`, `rbq10_trot`, `rbq10_trot_run`.

Trained your own policy with [Isaac Gym](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/simulator/rbq-gym.html) or [Isaac Lab](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/simulator/rbq-lab.html)?  
Point `-p` at the exported directory (`policy.onnx` + `info.json`).

## State machine

| State | How to enter | What happens |
|-------|-------------|-------------|
| Idle | (default) | Mirrors the stack's final joint reference |
| Motion | `x` or `z` | Cosine-interpolates to ready / ground posture |
| Control | `c` | Runs ONNX policy at 100 Hz, publishes joint references |

→ **C++ version**: [Low Level (C++)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-cpp/low-level.html)

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-python/quick-start.html
================================================================================

# RBQ Python SDK — Quick Start

Run a Python SDK example in 3 steps.

## 1. Clone and install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/RainbowRobotics/RBQ.git
cd RBQ

# Install the Python SDK
cd rbq_sdk/python
pip install -e .
cd ../..
```

## 2. Start the simulator (skip for real hardware)

The simulator runs in Docker — Docker is the only thing to install, and the script offers to install it when it is missing. The first run takes a few minutes to build its image. See [MuJoCo](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/simulator/mujoco.html).

```bash
bash scripts/sim.bash --no-gui
```

In the **RBQ** app on the same PC — started there, the desktop app finds this simulator on its own: **Control** → **Auto Start** → `STAND`. See [Control home](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/control-home.html).

## 3. Run an example

```bash
cd rbq_sdk/python/example/sport

# Terminal CLI
python3 rbq_sport_client.py

# Joystick control
python3 rbq_sport_client_joy.py
```

Both examples default to the loopback interface (`lo`) — the same one the
simulator and the on-robot stack use — so no argument is needed while the whole
stack runs on this PC.

**On a real robot**, pass the interface that reaches it as the first argument:

```bash
python3 rbq_sport_client.py eth0
```

Check your interface name with `ip link`.

## Examples overview

| Example | What it does |
|---------|-------------|
| [Sport Client →](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-python/sport-client.html) | Terminal CLI — test any command |
| [Sport Client (Joy) →](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-python/sport-client-joy.html) | Gamepad — full button mapping |

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-python/sport-client-joy.html
================================================================================

# Sport Client Joystick (Python) — Quick Start

**Source**: `rbq_sdk/python/example/sport/rbq_sport_client_joy.py`

Gamepad-driven robot control via Python SportClient. Single event loop at 10 Hz.

## Install

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/python
pip install -e .
```

## Run

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/python/example/sport
python3 rbq_sport_client_joy.py [networkInterface] [joystickPath]

# Simulator / on-robot stack — interface defaults to lo
python3 rbq_sport_client_joy.py

# Real robot — pass the interface that reaches it
python3 rbq_sport_client_joy.py eth0
python3 rbq_sport_client_joy.py eth0 /dev/input/js1
```

## Gamepad layout (Logitech F710 / Xbox)

### Button chords

| Hold + Press | Action |
|-------------|--------|
| **L2 + B** | E-stop (Damp) |
| **L2 + A** × 1 | StandUp |
| **L2 + A** × 2 | StandDown |
| **START** | Default gait |
| **L2 + START** | Running mode |
| **L2 + X** | Recovery stand |
| **R1 + X** | Climb |
| **BACK** | Stop |

### Double-click (400 ms)

| Button | Action |
|--------|--------|
| X × 2 | Left-side gait |
| Y × 2 | Right-side gait |

### Sticks (when no button)

| Axis | Command | Max |
|------|---------|-----|
| L stick forward | vel_x | ±1.0 m/s |
| L stick left | vel_y | ±0.5 m/s |
| R stick left | vyaw | ±1.0 rad/s |

→ **Full reference**: [Sport Client Joystick (Python)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/python/sport-client-joy.html)

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-python/sport-client.html
================================================================================

# Sport Client (Python) — Quick Start

**Source**: `rbq_sdk/python/example/sport/rbq_sport_client.py`

Python terminal CLI for sending SportClient commands.

## Install

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/python

```

## Run

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/python/example/sport
python3 rbq_sport_client.py [networkInterface]

# Simulator / on-robot stack — interface defaults to lo
python3 rbq_sport_client.py

# Real robot — pass the interface that reaches it

```

## Usage

```
Input "list " to list all test option ...
list            ← print all commands
balance_stand   ← execute by name
1               ← execute by ID
```

## Key commands

| ID | Name | What it does |
|----|------|-------------|
| 0 | `damp` | E-stop |
| 1 | `balance_stand` | Standing |
| 4 | `recovery_stand` | Stand up from fall |
| 5 | `move` | Rotate in place |
| 8 | `get_state` | Print robot state |
| 11 | `stand_up` | Lock standing joints |

# High Level Command — Quick Start (ROS2)

**Source**: `rbq_sdk/ros2/src/rbq_examples/src/rbq_high_level.cpp`

Publishes `HighLevelCommand` at 50 Hz over ROS 2.  
Select gaits from the terminal; control velocity with a joystick.

## Build

```bash
cd RBQ/rbq_sdk/ros2
rosdep install --from-paths src -y --ignore-src
colcon build --symlink-install
source install/setup.bash
```

## Run

```bash
ros2 run rbq_examples rbq_high_level [joystickPath]
# e.g.
ros2 run rbq_examples rbq_high_level
ros2 run rbq_examples rbq_high_level /dev/input/js1
```

Default joystick path is `/dev/input/js0`.

## Terminal usage

```
list              ← print the example's built-in list
stand             ← switch by name
3                 ← switch by ID (walk)
wave              ← switch to wave gait
```

## Supported gaits

| Name | ID | Notes |
|------|----|-------|
| `sit` | 0 | Sit down |
| `stand` | 1 | Default standing |
| `walk` | 3 | MPC trot gait |
| `stairs` | 4 | Stair-adaptive gait |
| `wave` | 5 | Slow walk gait |

> The example's built-in list also prints internal gaits that are not supported. Use only the gaits in the table above.

## Joystick velocity

| Axis | Command | Max |
|------|---------|-----|
| L stick forward/back | `vel_x` | ±1.2 m/s |
| L stick left/right | `vel_y` | ±0.5 m/s |
| R stick left/right | `omega_z` | ±60 deg/s |

Deadzone: 0.12. `omega_z` is in **deg/s**.

## ROS 2 topics used

| Direction | Topic | Message type |
|-----------|-------|--------------|
| Publish | `/rbq/cmd/high_level` | `rbq_msgs/msg/HighLevelCommand` |
| Publish | `/rbq/cmd/switch_control_mode` | `std_msgs/msg/Bool` |
| Publish | `/rbq/cmd/switch_gait` | `std_msgs/msg/Int8` |
| Subscribe | `/rbq/robot_status` | `rbq_msgs/msg/RobotStatus` (best-effort QoS) |

`HighLevelCommand` posture/velocity fields (`roll`, `pitch`, `yaw`, `vel_x`, `vel_y`, `omega_z`, `delta_body_h`, `delta_foot_h`) are `float32`. See the [full field reference](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/ros/high-level.html).

## Important

At startup, `switch_control_mode = true` is sent once to enable HighLevel mode.  
Without this, the robot ignores `HighLevelCommand` and stays in joystick mode.

→ **Full reference**: [High Level Command (ROS2)](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/ros/high-level.html)

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/guides/sdk-ros/quick-start.html
================================================================================

# RBQ ROS2 SDK — Quick Start

Connect the RBQ robot to ROS 2 Humble in 4 steps.

## 1. Clone and install ROS

```bash
git clone https://github.com/RainbowRobotics/RBQ.git
cd RBQ

# Install ROS 2 Humble (first time) — https://docs.ros.org/en/humble/Installation/Ubuntu-Install-Debs.html
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y ros-humble-desktop \
    python3-colcon-common-extensions python3-rosdep \
    ros-humble-rmw-cyclonedds-cpp ros-humble-cyclonedds
sudo rosdep init && rosdep update
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
```

## 2. Build the ROS2 SDK

```bash
cd rbq_sdk/ros2
rosdep install --from-paths src -y --ignore-src
colcon build --symlink-install
source install/setup.bash
cd ../..
```

## 3. Run

**Simulation:**
```bash
source rbq_sdk/ros2/install/setup.bash
bash scripts/sim.bash
```

**Real robot:**

The robot's onboard software (`Network`) already speaks ROS 2-compatible DDS — there is **no driver node to launch**. Just source the workspace and configure DDS (next step) to reach the robot over the network.

```bash
source rbq_sdk/ros2/install/setup.bash
```

> The legacy `rbq_driver` node and `scripts/start_ros_driver.bash` are removed — the script is now a deprecated no-op.

## 4. DDS setup (developer PC ↔ robot Wi-Fi)

Set in the terminal you use for `ros2 topic` commands:

```bash
export CYCLONEDDS_URI='<CycloneDDS><Domain><Id>0</Id><General><Interfaces><NetworkInterface name="wlp4s0"/></Interfaces></General></Domain></CycloneDDS>'
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp
```

Replace `wlp4s0` with your Wi-Fi interface (`ifconfig` to check).

## Quick command test

```bash
# Enable HighLevel Command mode
ros2 topic pub --once /rbq/cmd/switch_control_mode std_msgs/msg/Bool "{data: true}"

# Stand up
ros2 topic pub --once /rbq/cmd/switch_gait std_msgs/msg/Int8 "{data: 1}"

# Switch to walk mode
ros2 topic pub --once /rbq/cmd/switch_gait std_msgs/msg/Int8 "{data: 3}"

# Walk forward 0.3 m/s — walks about 1 second, then stops on its own
ros2 topic pub --once /rbq/cmd/high_level rbq_msgs/msg/HighLevelCommand \
'{vel_x: 0.3, vel_y: 0.0, omega_z: 0.0, gait_state: 3, gait_transition: false}'

# Check topics
ros2 topic list
```

::: tip Stopping after 1 second is expected
As a safety measure, velocities are **zeroed once the last command is older than 1 second**.
A command sent with `--once` therefore walks for about a second and stops on its own — which is
the safe behavior for a quick test. To keep the robot walking, publish periodically, e.g.
`ros2 topic pub -r 50 …` (stop with <kbd>Ctrl+C</kbd>).
:::

## List available topics

```bash
source rbq_sdk/ros2/install/setup.bash
ros2 topic list
```

→ **Full ROS2 reference**: [ROS2 SDK Overview](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/ros/overview.html)
