# PTZ camera

::: tip
This panel appears only on robots fitted with the optional PTZ camera unit. `CCTV` is listed when the robot reports the PTZ color camera. `Thermal` and `PTZ Mix` also need the thermal sensor, so a PTZ unit without one shows `CCTV` only. If all three are missing from the viewport source list, no PTZ unit was detected.
:::

## Opening the panel

There is no separate PTZ screen. Switch the viewport source to `CCTV`, `Thermal`, or `PTZ Mix` and the PTZ control panel floats over the video. Switch to any other source and it disappears. You control the camera while looking at its picture.


## Pan / tilt

![PTZ panel over the viewport](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/home-ptz.pc.en.png)

Drag the small joystick at the top of the panel to move the camera: left/right pans, up/down tilts. The camera keeps moving as long as you hold the stick and stops when you release it. Use small, slow inputs to settle on a target. The `Sensitivity` slider at the bottom of the panel — default 60 %, minimum 10 % — scales the stick output. It stays separate from the robot's own joystick sensitivity because gimbal work needs finer steps.

## Zoom

Optical zoom has five fixed steps — the camera does not accept values in between:

- `1x`, `3x`, `8x`, `16x`, `32x` — tap a step button to jump straight to it.
- The `Zoom` slider above the buttons scrubs through the same five steps, and the current step appears to its right.

## Center

`Center` returns the camera to its home position: pan and tilt to the middle of their range and zoom fully out. The `Zoom` slider and step buttons do not follow this reset — tap `1x` if you want the panel to match the camera again. Use it when you have lost track of where the camera is pointing.

## Face temperature

On the `PTZ Mix` source only, a `FaceTemp OFF` / `FaceTemp ON` button appears next to `Center`. Turn it on to read the temperature of detected faces from the combined color + thermal view. Switching to any other source turns it off automatically.

## Moving the panel

The panel starts to the left of the `PTZ` row in the OBSERVE card, so it is next to the button that opens it. Drag it by the handle in its top-right corner to any spot that does not hide what you need to see — the bottom corners are reserved for the virtual joysticks. On a short screen the panel is pulled back inside the viewport, because a handle off the screen would leave you no way to move it.

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/settings.html
================================================================================

# Settings

Settings come in two sets. Each one lays its sections out as chips across the top — icons only on a phone.

- **Robot settings** belong to the selected robot. Open them with the `Robot settings` tile on the hub. Sections: `Calibration`, `Power`, `Payload setup`, `Software update`. The title reads `Robot` with the robot's name and serial.
- **App settings** belong to this device. Open them with the gear button at the top right of the hub or any sub-screen. Sections: `Gamepad`, `App settings`. The title reads `App` with the device and app version.

On every settings screen the logo at the top left returns to the hub, and the gamepad button next to it goes straight to the control screen. That button works only while a robot is connected or the sim is running.

- Connecting to a robot is done from the robot list on the hub — see [Connection](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/connection.html).
- `Gamepad` is covered in [Gamepad](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/gamepad.html).
- `Software update` is covered in [Software Update](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/software-update.html).

This page covers the remaining four sections. Operators can use all of them, and rows that need developer mode are marked.

## Calibration {#calibration}

![Calibration section](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/settings-cal.pc.en.png)

::: warning
Every calibration here must be run with the robot on flat ground and **stationary**. The IMU and ZMP rows are blocked while the robot is walking, has fallen, or is not reporting its state, and each one asks `Run calibration?` before it sends the command. `Joint home-pose setup` has its own confirmation. Do not touch the robot until the calibration has finished.
:::

### IMU Calibration

| Row | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Accelerometer calib (ACC)` | Field correction of accelerometer drift. Run it **while the robot is sitting**, on level ground; it averages the gravity magnitude for about 2 s and stores the factor. |
| `IMU roll/pitch zero` | Makes the current posture the level reference. Takes about half a second — if the robot is tilted when you run it, all later control will be off. |
| `Gyro Bias Calibration` | Resets the IMU, waits for the values to settle, then measures the gyro again — about 5 s, **while the robot is sitting**. When it finishes it reports all three axes and whether each one is within the limit. If the bias is still over the limit, hold the robot completely still and run it again. |

Press `Run`, then confirm `Run` in the dialog. When a row is blocked, the app tells you why, and if it can clear the block itself, a button appears next to `Run`: `Sit` when the robot needs to sit, `Stand` when it needs to stand, and `Auto Start` when control is off, which asks first. You get no such button while the robot has fallen, is docking, or is not reporting.

`IMU roll/pitch zero` shows the current roll and pitch under the level in its dialog. A progress dialog follows while it runs. It ends with `Success` only when roll and pitch both come back within 1° — if the robot is still tilted, it reads `The zero may not have taken effect` instead, and you put the robot on flat ground and run it again.

### ZMP Calibration

`Auto-calibrate ZMP offset` finds the center-of-mass offset automatically. The robot must be in STAND on flat ground. It walks one step to square up its legs, then takes up to 60 s to converge. Once the offset converges, the robot saves it on its own and returns to STAND. The panel shows the progress and a completion message.

### Joint Calibration

Re-establishes the leg joints' zeros and offsets. Run it with the robot **sitting**.

| Row | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Joint home-pose setup` | Hold the home pose with the jig, then store it as the joint zero — four legs |
| `DQ offset calibration` | `Not available yet` — the row is reserved and cannot be pressed |

`Joint home-pose setup` opens two dialogs: first the notice (*This rewrites the joint zeros — running it without the jig, or with the pose off, leaves the robot booting on wrong zeros*), then the per-leg screen. On that screen, pick the joints you want to set; the ones you pick move to the target pose in the 3D view on the left. Fit the jig, hold that pose, and press `Save LEG{n} {g} home pose`. Writing the zero switches control off (BOARD_RESET), so sit the robot down first — it will collapse if it is standing. The jig is required.

If the motor boards do not answer, the row is blocked with *No communication with the motor boards — turn the 48 V drive (LEGS) power on and run it again*; that rail is in [Maintenance](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/maintenance.html).

### Camera Calibration

> **What developer mode adds here** is collected on [Developer mode](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/developer-mode.html#settings).

### Docking calibration

The bottom of the Calibration section holds the auto-docking alignment parameters: `Offset X (m)`, `Offset Y (m)`, `Req Count`, `Try Count`.

- `Reload` re-reads the values from the robot.
- `Defaults` fills the fields with factory defaults — nothing is saved until you press `Apply`.
- `Apply` writes the values to the robot and reads them back.

## Power

This section switches the auxiliary rails you use day to day. The toggles show the actual PDU state the robot reports, so a change can take about a second to show up. Until the first rail state arrives, the toggles stay disabled.

**12 V toggles** (one tap): `Speaker amp (12V)`, `CCTV (12V)`, `Thermal (12V)`, `IR LED (12V)`.

**48 V rails** (two-step): `ARM · ADDON (48V)` and `EXTERN (48V)` each show the live voltage and a `Turn off` / `Turn on` button. Pressing it opens `Turn this off?` or `Turn this on?`. Confirm to switch.

::: warning
`ARM · ADDON (48V)` is one PDU port shared by the arm and the add-on. Turning it off also cuts arm power — make sure the arm is stopped first.
:::

Camera, comm, Vision PC, and LEGS (48 V) power, along with LiDAR and system reboot, are not here — switching any of them off breaks the connection or drops the robot. They live in [Maintenance](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/maintenance.html) (developer mode).

## Payload setup {#robot-parameters}

![Robot parameters section](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/settings-robot.pc.en.png)

`Payload Configuration` describes what is mounted on the robot so the walking dynamics can account for it.

1. The robot reports 13 payload slots. Check a slot to mark it as mounted and enter its mass and center of mass (X, Y, Z).
2. The footer shows the total mass and combined center of mass, and warns when the total exceeds the limit.
3. Press `Set Payload` and confirm with `Apply` (`Get` re-reads the slots from the robot and discards your edits). The confirmation shows the number of mounted slots and the totals; unchecked slots are sent with mass 0. The new values reach the walking dynamics right away, ramped in over one to two seconds.

`Help` expands a short guide above the table. Robots without the payload slot API show a notice asking for a robot software update instead.

## App settings

![App settings section](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/settings-app.pc.en.png)

These settings belong to the app, not the robot.

| Row | Options |
|---|---|
| `Theme` | `Dark` / `Light` |
| `Language / 언어` | `Korean` / `English` — applies immediately |
| `Joystick sensitivity` | Slider — input response curve |
| `Keep screen on` | Toggle — keeps the screen awake while controlling |
| `Deadzone` | Slider — center range ignored by the joystick |
| `Gyro widget` | Toggle — roll/pitch attitude display |
| `Fullscreen` | Toggle — browser only |
| `Low-signal warning` | Toggle — top warning banner when Wi-Fi signal drops below `Warning threshold` (slider, shown while enabled) |
| `Warning beep (Notify BEEP)` | Toggle — short beep on warnings (web only) |
| `Low battery beep` | Toggle — beeps when the robot battery is low; `Warning beep (Notify BEEP)` must be on (web only) |
| `UI scale` | Desktop app only — `Auto`, 100 % to 200 % |

### Developer mode {#developer-mode}

The `Developer mode` toggle is in the profile menu — the round button at the top right, next to the gear. As a guest, turn on `Developer mode` and enter the password. Turning it off puts you back at the operator level. While you are logged in with an access code (`Log in with access code` in the same menu) the toggle is not shown, because the account decides the level.

Developer mode adds the `Maintenance` tile on the hub, the developer rows above, and the `AI motion` and `Position control` groups in the `Select motion` grid.

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/software-update.html
================================================================================

# Software Update

Open **Robot settings → Software update**. The section updates two things: the software running on the robot, and this app itself.

![Software update section](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/settings-sw.pc.en.png)

## Robot software

The top of the panel shows two cards:

- `Current robot` · Motion — `Version`, `Branch`, `Commit`, `Build` as reported by the robot.
- `Update file` — the package you are about to send: `Selected` file name, its `Version`, `Size`, and the `Target`.

### Choosing a package

There are two ways to get a package onto the device.

**Online** — the list below the cards shows the versions published for this app's release channel (`Online update` · `internet required`). Press `Check versions` (or `Refresh`) to fetch the list, then `Download` on the version you want. The download pulls the robot package onto this device, along with the app build on desktop. The row then shows the package size, plus `Latest` and `In use` badges where they apply. Downloaded files stay on the device, so you can download on the internet network and switch to the robot network before sending. `Remove` deletes a downloaded package. The `Release notes` under the list cover the selected version, or the version the robot is running when nothing is selected.

**From USB or a file** — press `Load from USB or file`. The system file picker opens (a USB OTG drive shows up there like any other storage). Pick the package file; it must be named `RBQ-<version>.tar.gz` (the robot also accepts the `RBQ-<version>.zip` package). The `Update file` card fills in with the file's name, version, and size.

### Target

`Target` selects which robot PC receives the package: `Motion` (the robot IP you are connected to) or `Vision`. Vision matters only on older robots that have a separate vision PC. If the robot has no vision IP set — the `Vision IP` field in its profile on the hub, or `Vision PC IP (optional)` when you add it by address, both [developer mode](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/developer-mode.html) — the app falls back to the default vision address and says so in a note.

### Sending

1. Press `Send robot software`.
2. The dialog `Send to the robot?` lists the file, size, and target. If the file name follows `RBQ-<version>.tar.gz`, the dialog warns that the robot will unpack and deploy it as soon as the transfer completes, replacing the running software. The dialog says files with any other name are only stored on the robot, but current robot software refuses them outright with a "Rejected file name" error — send only properly named packages.
3. Press `Send`. The progress bar shows the percentage, and `Cancel` aborts the transfer.
4. On success the panel shows `✓ Transfer complete` and asks `Deploy transfer complete — reboot now?`. With a `Vision` target the dialog only says the vision PC cannot be rebooted from the app and closes with `Check`.

### Reboot

Robot software takes effect only after you reboot the robot. For a `Motion` target the reboot prompt offers `Later` and `Reboot now`.

::: warning
Rebooting cuts motor power and the robot will sag to the ground. The robot must be in the **sitting** state before you reboot — sit it down first and make sure it is resting on the floor, and do not move it during the reboot. If the robot is standing it ignores the reboot command, and the app shows no error. The app connection drops while the robot restarts. Reconnect afterwards and check that `Current robot` shows the new version.
:::

The vision PC cannot be rebooted from the app. If the target was `Vision`, reboot that PC by hand.

## This app

The **GUI Version** line shows the version of the app you are running, followed by a badge:

- no badge — a release build,
- `NIGHTLY` — a nightly build (its list shows `Nightly builds` · `last 10 kept` instead of the release list),
- `LOCAL` — a local build with no release channel; it does not check for updates.

Next to it, `Matches robot` (with a check mark) or `Differs from robot` compares the app version with the robot version. Keeping the two the same is the intended pairing.

Once the version list has loaded, an update button appears if a newer app is available:

- `Update in store` — store installs (Google Play / App Store). The store app opens; install from there.
- `<version> Update` — APK and desktop installs. The app downloads the build and installs it (Android hands it to the system installer; desktop switches to the new build). `You're on the latest version` is shown when nothing newer exists.

On desktop, `Install online` registers a build you downloaded but never installed, and `Use this build` switches to any downloaded build in the list.

Nightly builds only see nightly releases and release builds only see releases — the channel is fixed when the app is built.

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/hardware/coordinate-frames.html
================================================================================

# Coordinate Frames (TF)

This page collects the **base-to-sensor transform matrices (TF)** for every sensor mounted on
the RBQ. Each matrix is a 4×4 homogeneous transform from the robot base frame to the sensor
frame; translation components are in **meters (m)**.

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>These are <strong>fixed mounting transforms</strong>. Transforms that change at runtime (<code>odom → base_link</code>, leg joints, and so on) are broadcast by the robot on <code>/tf</code> — see the <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/software/sdk/ros/topics.html#tf">ROS 2 topic reference</a>.</p>
</div>
</div>

### MID-360S {#mid-360s}

Values for the MID-360S variant. The tilt is the same ±35° as the MID-360, but the sensor is
mounted rotated 90° about its vertical axis — the connector faces the robot's left on the
front LiDAR and the robot's right on the rear LiDAR.

# Rail & spring nut

The robot uses **rails** for mounting optional hardware such as **PTZ cameras**, **LiDAR** units, and related brackets. **Spring nuts** inserted into the rail slot provide threaded anchor points for bolts.

## Purchase links

| Region | MISUMI product page |
|--------|----------------------|
| South Korea | [SHNTP5-5 (kr.misumi-ec.com)](https://kr.misumi-ec.com/vona2/detail/110302608410/?HissuCode=SHNTP5-5&PNSearch=SHNTP5-5&searchFlow=results2products&list=PageSearchResult) |
| United States | [SHNTP5-5 (us.misumi-ec.com)](https://us.misumi-ec.com/vona2/detail/110302247640/?PNSearch=SHNTP5-5&HissuCode=SHNTP5-5&seriesCode=110302247640&tab=drawingAndSpecifications&Page=1) |

## Inserting a spring nut

1. **Insert at an angle.** Slide the spring nut **diagonally** into the rail slot so it enters the internal channel.
2. **Press the part that sticks out.** A portion of the nut may sit **proud of the slot**; press it so the nut seats fully in the channel.
3. **Align with the rail.** Adjust the nut so it is **aligned with the slot** and can slide along the rail as needed.

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/insert-1.png' alt='Insert spring nut diagonally into the rail' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 1 - diagonal insert</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/insert-2.png' alt='Press the portion protruding outside the rail' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 2 - press the protruding section</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/insert-3.png' alt='Align the nut with the rail slot' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 3 - align with the slot</figcaption>
</figure>

## Removing a spring nut

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p><strong>Tool diameter</strong></p>
<p>Use a rigid rod <strong>no larger than 4 mm</strong> in diameter. A thicker tool can damage the nut or mar the rail slot.</p>
</div>
</div>

1. **Insert a rod into the nut.** Pass a **rigid rod** (**≤ 4 mm** diameter) through the hole in the spring nut.
2. **Push to one wall.** Push the nut **against one inner wall** of the rail slot.
3. **Twist and lift.** While holding it against that wall, **twist and lift** the nut toward the **opposite** side of the slot so it can clear the profile and release from the rail.
4. **Remove.** Withdraw the nut from the slot.

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/remove-1.png' alt='Insert rod into spring nut hole' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 1 - rod through the hole</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/remove-2.png' alt='Push nut against one wall of the rail' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 2 - push to one wall</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/remove-3.png' alt='Twist and lift away from the wall' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 3 - twist and lift</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/remove-4.png' alt='Remove spring nut from rail' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto;" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">Step 4 - remove</figcaption>
</figure>

# External Port Information

## Overall External Port Panel

There are two panel layouts — **version 1** and **version 2** — and which one your robot
has depends on the robot. The quickest way to tell them apart is the pair of USB-C ports
on the right edge: version 1 labels them **VISION / MOTION**, version 2 labels them
**U-PC / R-PC**. They are the same two ports — version 2 names the PC each one reaches
instead of its role.

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>The panel layout can differ between versions. Please <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/support/">contact us</a> if you are unsure which one your robot has.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="rbq-compare">
  <figure id="panel-v1">
    <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/interface/port-panel-v1.png' alt='External port panel, version 1' />
    <figcaption>Version 1</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure id="panel-v2">
    <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/interface/port-panel-v2.png' alt='External port panel, version 2' />
    <figcaption>Version 2</figcaption>
  </figure>
</div>

### Ports by version {#ports-by-version}

| Port | Version 1 | Version 2 |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Power | `POWER` | `POWER` |
| Power · CAN | `PWR-CAN` | `PWR/CAN` |
| Power · LAN | `12V-LAN` ×3 | `12V/LAN` ×3 |
| LiDAR | `LiDAR` | No dedicated port — use `12V/LAN` |
| Emergency stop | `EMO` | `EMO` |
| USB-C (direct to PC) | `VISION`, `MOTION` | `U-PC`, `R-PC` |

## Charging & Power Switch

Both versions carry the same three elements — the power port with its cover, the power
button, and the robot status lights — but lay them out differently.

<div class="rbq-compare">
  <figure>
    <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/interface/power-switch-v1.png' alt='Charging and power switch, version 1' />
    <figcaption>Version 1</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure>
    <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/interface/power-switch-v2.png' alt='Charging and power switch, version 2' />
    <figcaption>Version 2</figcaption>
  </figure>
</div>

| Element | Version 1 | Version 2 |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Power port cover | Hinged flip cover | Screw-down round cover |
| Robot status lights | Horizontal strip above the power port | Vertical strip beside the power button |
| Power button | Below the power port | Bottom left, next to the status lights |

================================================================================

# GNSS · RTK (satellite positioning)

With a GNSS receiver attached, the robot passes satellite positioning data through **as raw NMEA
sentences**. The robot's `GPS` program reads the sentences from the receiver and republishes them
unchanged on a ROS 2 topic.

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>GNSS needs <strong>robot software that includes the <code>GPS</code> program</strong> and a GNSS receiver. For receivers and the LTE/GPS module see <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/product-descriptions/accessories.html#wifi-lte-gps-module">Accessories</a>.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Topic {#topic}

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Topic | `/rbq/gps/nmea` |
| Type | [`nmea_msgs/Sentence`](https://docs.ros.org/en/noetic/api/nmea_msgs/html/msg/Sentence.html) |
| Direction | Pub (robot → client) |

The message has just two fields.

| Field | Contents |
|---|---|
| `header.stamp` | The time the robot **read** the sentence (not the UTC inside it) |
| `header.frame_id` | `gps` — the receiver (antenna) frame |
| `sentence` | One raw NMEA 0183 line (starts with `$`, checksum included) |

Sentences are **not processed**. Parsing is left to the subscriber; NMEA is a standard format with
parsers in most languages.

```bash
ros2 topic echo /rbq/gps/nmea
```

<figure style="text-align: center; margin: 1rem 0;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/interface/gnss-topic-echo.png' alt='ros2 topic echo /rbq/gps/nmea output showing GNRMC, GNGGA and GNGST sentences' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 100%; height: auto; border-radius: 6px;" />
  <figcaption style="margin-top: 0.5rem; text-align: center; color: var(--vp-c-text-2, #666); font-size: 0.95em;">[ Live output — the three sentences arrive in sequence each cycle ]</figcaption>
</figure>

## The three sentences {#sentences}

Of everything the receiver emits, only these three types are published; the rest are dropped. The
`GN` prefix means the fix combines several constellations (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou).

### `$GNRMC` — position, speed, time {#gnrmc}

```
$GNRMC,<UTC time>,<status>,<latitude>,<N/S>,<longitude>,<E/W>,<speed>,<course>,<UTC date>,<magnetic variation>,<E/W>,<mode>,<nav status>*<checksum>
```

| Field | Contents |
|---|---|
| UTC time · date | When the fix was taken |
| Status | Data valid (`A`) or not (`V`) |
| Latitude · longitude | Position |
| Speed | Speed over ground (knots) |
| Course | Heading, relative to true north |
| Magnetic variation | Difference between true and magnetic north |
| Mode · nav status | How the position was determined, and the navigation status |

### `$GNGGA` — fix quality and altitude {#gngga}

```
$GNGGA,<UTC time>,<latitude>,<N/S>,<longitude>,<E/W>,<fix quality>,<satellites>,<HDOP>,<altitude>,M,<geoid separation>,M,<DGPS age>,<station ID>*<checksum>
```

| Field | Contents |
|---|---|
| Fix quality | **This is where you check the RTK state** — see the table below |
| Satellites | Number of satellites used for the fix |
| HDOP | Horizontal dilution of precision — lower is better |
| Altitude | Above mean sea level |
| Geoid separation | Difference between the ellipsoid and the geoid |
| DGPS age · station ID | How long since the last correction (RTCM) and which base station sent it |

The fix-quality values are NMEA 0183 standard.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | No fix |
| `1` | Standalone GPS fix |
| `2` | DGPS — corrections applied |
| `4` | **RTK fixed** — integer ambiguities resolved, the most accurate |
| `5` | **RTK float** — ambiguities not resolved |

### `$GNGST` — position error estimates {#gngst}

```
$GNGST,<UTC time>,<RMS>,<semi-major σ>,<semi-minor σ>,<orientation>,<latitude σ>,<longitude σ>,<altitude σ>*<checksum>
```

| Field | Contents |
|---|---|
| RMS | RMS of the range residuals |
| Semi-major · semi-minor σ · orientation | Standard deviations and bearing of the error ellipse |
| Latitude · longitude · altitude σ | Per-axis position error standard deviation (m) |

**This sentence is how you judge what RTK actually bought you.** Once the latitude and longitude σ
drop to centimetre level, RTK has locked in.

## Checking that it works {#verify}

1. **Is the topic flowing?** — run `ros2 topic echo /rbq/gps/nmea` and watch for sentences.
2. **Is there a fix?** — a fix quality of `0` in `$GNGGA` means no satellites yet. Move somewhere
   with open sky and wait a moment.
3. **Is RTK locked?** — check that the fix quality is `4` (fixed) or `5` (float), and that the
   latitude and longitude σ in `$GNGST` are small enough.

In **[Logs → Real Time](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/logs.html#real-time)**, filtering down to the `GPS` process shows the
connect and disconnect messages directly.

## When it does not work {#troubleshooting}

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| Nothing arrives on the topic | Check that the receiver is attached and powered, and that the robot can reach its address |
| It connects but no sentences appear | Anything outside `GNRMC`, `GNGGA` and `GNGST` is dropped. Enable those sentences in the receiver's own configuration |
| Fix quality never rises above `1` | No corrections (RTCM) are arriving. Check the DGPS age and station ID in `$GNGGA` |
| No fix indoors | GNSS needs a view of the sky. Indoors or between tall buildings there may be no fix, or a large error |

## Still stuck {#still-stuck}

Tell us the receiver model and a few lines of `ros2 topic echo /rbq/gps/nmea` output.

**→ [Support](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/support/)**

SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/network.html

# Network Configuration Diagram

The network layout differs from robot to robot. Two things vary:

- **Configuration** — the **research** layout keeps the User PC outside the robot and treats payloads as one generic LAN group. The **industrial** layout mounts the User PC inside the robot and wires each payload individually.
- **Router** — some robots have the router **integrated into the switch hub**, so the LTE/5G · Wi-Fi (Mesh) module connects straight to it. Others reach the network through a **separate external router**.

In every diagram, **R-PC** is the robot's motion PC and **U-PC** is the user PC. Green lines are LAN, orange lines are WAN.

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>The network layout can differ between versions. Please <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/support/">contact us</a> if you are unsure which one applies to your robot.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Research configuration

The U-PC sits outside the robot. LAN payloads — LiDAR, PTZ camera, RTK GPS and so on — share a single connection to the switch hub.

### Router integrated into the switch hub

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/interface/network-diagram-1.png' alt='Network configuration diagram, research configuration, router integrated into the switch hub' />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ Research · Router integrated ]</figcaption>
</figure>

### Separate external router

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/interface/network-diagram-4.png' alt='Network configuration diagram, research configuration, separate external router' />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ Research · External router ]</figcaption>
</figure>

## Industrial configuration

The U-PC is mounted inside the robot alongside the R-PC, and each payload — LiDAR 1, LiDAR 2, PTZ camera — has its own connection to the switch hub.

### Router integrated into the switch hub

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/interface/network-diagram-2.png' alt='Network configuration diagram, industrial configuration, router integrated into the switch hub' />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ Industrial · Router integrated ]</figcaption>
</figure>

### Separate external router

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/interface/network-diagram-3.png' alt='Network configuration diagram, industrial configuration, separate external router' />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ Industrial · External router ]</figcaption>
</figure>

On this layout LiDAR 2 connects through the router rather than directly to the switch hub.

## Network details

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Wi-Fi | 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz |
| Network switch speed | Gigabit Ethernet (1 Gbps) |
| Access point | `192.168.0.1` |

## Onboard PCs and IP addresses

Every robot ships with the Motion PC (R-PC). The User PC (U-PC) is an option — your robot may
not have one. **The U-PC's address depends on where it is mounted.**

| PC | IP | Role | Fitted | User access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Motion PC (R-PC) | `192.168.0.10` | Robot control | Standard | No |
| User PC (U-PC) — mounted inside the robot | `192.168.0.12` | Your development work | Option | Yes |
| User PC (U-PC) — outside the robot | `192.168.0.13` | Your development work | Option | Yes |

The Motion PC runs the robot itself and is not user-accessible. Do your development work on
the U-PC.

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">If the U-PC does not respond</p>
<p>The U-PC uses <code>192.168.0.12</code> when it is mounted inside the robot, and <code>192.168.0.13</code> when it sits outside. If you cannot connect, attach a monitor to the U-PC and check its current IP. If it is using a different address, set it statically to the address above.</p>
</div>
</div>

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/port-power.html
================================================================================

# Powering the external ports

If a payload wired into an external port does nothing, the usual reason is that **the port's power
is off**. Plugging the connector in does not energise the port — **you switch it on in the app**.

Wiring and pin assignments are in [External ports](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/external-port.html); the cables are
listed under [Accessories](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/product-descriptions/accessories.html#payload-cabling).

## Where to switch it on {#where}

| Screen | Access | What lives there |
|---|---|---|
| **Robot settings → Power** | Everyone | The auxiliary power you switch during everyday operation |
| **Maintenance → Power / System** | [developer mode](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/developer-mode.html) (level 2 or higher) | The above, plus rails that cut the connection or the robot's stance |

For an ordinary payload, **Robot settings → Power** is all you need.

![Robot settings → Power](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/settings-pwr.pc.en.png)

## Switching on a 48 V port {#48v}

Ports that carry raw battery voltage — `POWER` (2-pin) and `PWR-CAN` (4-pin) — sit on the 48 V rails.

1. Open **Robot settings → Power**.
2. Press **`Turn on`** on the `EXTERN (48V)` row — the power that goes out to the external expansion
   ports.
3. Confirm with **`Turn on`** in the `Turn this on?` dialog.
4. Check that the **live voltage** on that row comes up.

If your add-on sits on `ARM · ADDON (48V)`, switch that row instead.

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p><code>ARM · ADDON (48V)</code> is <strong>one PDU port shared</strong> by the arm and the add-on. Turning this rail off also cuts arm power, so make sure the arm is stopped before you switch it.</p>
</div>
</div>

The 48 V rails put out **raw battery voltage**, which moves between 42.0 V and 58.4 V with the state
of charge. Add your own converter if the payload needs a regulated supply.

## Switching on a 12 V device {#12v}

Devices that run on 12 V — cameras and lighting — have a per-device toggle; one tap switches it.

| Toggle | What it powers |
|---|---|
| `Speaker amp (12V)` | Walkie-talkie audio output — silent while off |
| `CCTV (12V)` | The color camera of the PTZ unit |
| `Thermal (12V)` | The thermal camera of the PTZ unit |
| `IR LED (12V)` | Night illumination |

`LiDAR (12V)`, `Cameras (5V)`, `Audio · USB hub (5V)`, `Vision PC (12V)` and `Comms (12V)` cut
driving, video or the connection itself, so they live under **Maintenance → Power / System**
([developer mode](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/developer-mode.html)).

## It is on but still does not work {#not-working}

- **The toggle is grayed out and will not press** — the rail state has not arrived yet. Check the
  robot connection first ([Connection](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/connection.html)).
- **It does not flip immediately** — the toggle shows the **actual state** the robot's PDU reports,
  and that takes about a second to come back.
- **The voltage does not come up** — check that the connector is seated and the cable is intact
  ([Connector handling](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/maintenance/connector.html)).
- **Power is present but the device stays off** — check you are within the per-port current limit:
  `POWER` 5 A, `PWR-CAN` 10 A, `12V/LAN` 2–3 A
  ([pin map](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/external-port.html#user-port-pin-map)).

## Still stuck {#still-stuck}

Tell us which port you wired what into, and the voltage shown on the power screen.

**→ [Support](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/support/)**

SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/maintenance/battery.html

# Battery Replacement

## How to detach batteries

<div class="sb sb-danger">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">DANGER</p>
<p><strong>Bare-hand contact</strong> with battery terminals or connectors can cause shock, short circuit, burns, or fire. Always wear <strong>insulating gloves</strong> when detaching or attaching. Confirm power is fully off.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Before detaching, confirm the RBQ10 is <strong>sitting down</strong> and <strong>powered off</strong>. Otherwise the robot may move or fall, which can escalate to a more severe incident.</p>
</div>
</div>

The batteries are located on the sides of the RBQ10.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/bat-1.png' alt='Battery location and side covers' />
</figure>

Before opening the latches of the RBQ10, the front legs must be lifted up for clearance.

<div class="sb sb-warning">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">WARNING</p>
<p>When lifting the legs or operating the latches and battery cover, keep <strong>fingers and hands clear of gaps</strong> between legs, body, and cover. Pulling or pushing a lever while your hand is in the gap can cause injury. <strong>Support or hold</strong> the part with one hand and operate levers and covers with the other only.</p>
</div>
</div>

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/bat-2.png' alt='Battery latch levers and detaching' />
</figure>

The levers are on the sides of the battery latches and pulling all four of them releases the battery from the body. After releasing the latches, pull the battery cover to detach the battery.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/bat-3.png' alt='Battery removal step' />
</figure>

## How to attach batteries

To attach the batteries, push the battery into the robot body and place the hook into the groove. Then, firmly press the levers to fix the battery.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/bat-4.png' alt='Battery installation and locking' />
</figure>

# Stand & Bumper Replacement

The stand that supports the body of the RBQ10 when it is in a standby sitting position, and the front and rear bumpers that absorb impact when the robot falls, wear out with use and need to be replaced. The replacement method is as follows, so please refer to it if necessary.

## Stand replacement

The stand of the RBQ10 consists of M4x10mm hex-wrench bolts and M4 flat washers. If any parts are lost during disassembly, you can purchase replacements of the same specifications.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/stand-bumper-1.png' alt='Stand and bumper replacement 1' />
</figure>

### Step 1. Unscrew the bolt using a 3mm hex wrench.

### Step 2. Pull out the urethane stand and replace it with a new component.

### Step 3. Fasten the bolt. (Apply Loctite 243 to the bolt thread)

## Front & rear bumpers

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/stand-bumper-2.png' alt='Stand and bumper replacement 2' />
</figure>

3 sets of M3x10mm bolts and M4 flat washers attach the bumper to the robot.

Use a 2.5mm hexagonal wrench to loosen the bolts.

# Connector Attachment/Detachment

The RBQ10 interface connector uses MOCO's F-series waterproof connector. Once the connector is engaged, it cannot be disconnected by vibration or pulling the wire. To remove the connector, you need to hold the handle and pull it to safely detach it without damage.

### Step 1. Grab the handle.

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Applying force to the wires outside the handle area may cause damage.</p>
</div>
</div>

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/connector-1.png' alt='Connector detachment 1' />
</figure>

### Step 2. Align the red dots and press the connector handle until it clicks.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/connector-2.png' alt='Connector detachment 2' />
</figure>


### Step 3. Check connection.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/connector-3.png' alt='Connector detachment 3' />
</figure>

# Leg module Attachment/Detachment

This manual explains the disassembly and assembly sequence of the RBQ10 leg module. The instructions are based on the front left leg, and since the other legs have a symmetrical structure, the same method should be used for the disassembly and assembly process.

<b>Fastening specification</b>

  <tr>
    <th>Parameter</th>
    <th>Specification</th>

    <td>4mm</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Q’ty</td>
    <td>6 bolts in total</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Spring washer</td>
    <td>M5</td>
  </tr>
</table>

### Step 2. Pull the leg module outward after the bolts are unscrewed.

## Leg module assembly

The leg com-wire must be coiled once before assembly. If it is assembled without coiling, the com-wire may get pinched and damaged between the leg and the upper and lower plates.

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>The spring washer for the bolts securing the leg is crucial for proper fastening. Be careful not to forget it during assembly.</p>
</div>
</div>

### Step 1. Coil the com-wire as shown in the picture below.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/leg-5.png' alt='Coiling the com-wire' />
</figure>

### Step 2. Align the red dots and press firmly to connect the com-wire.

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Pushing the com-wire may cause disconnection. Make sure to press the handle.</p>
</div>
</div>

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/leg-6.png' alt='Connector mating' />
</figure>

### Step 3. Insert the roll frame and reducer slot into the body frame.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/leg-7.png' alt='Insert roll frame' />
</figure>

### Step 4. Fasten the bolts. (Make sure to insert the M5 spring washers)

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/maintenance/leg-8.png' alt='Tighten leg module bolts' />

# Sheet Sticker Production

How to prepare the sheet stickers applied to the robot's exterior — **design, material and
placement**. Follow the steps below when preparing your print files.

<!-- 사진 교체 대상: custom_logo.png (KO/EN 공용) — 커스텀 로고 시트 스티커가 적용된 로봇 외장 예시. -->

## 1. Download the Illustrator template {#template}

Download the **RBQ sheet template (.ai)** from the **Sheet Sticker** folder in the
[shared SharePoint folder](https://rainbowco-my.sharepoint.com/:f:/g/personal/rbq_support_rainbow-robotics_com/IgCaa2vihZjyTKHTiEmmjzRsAbbKACHMA2OwCHlrDyH4y7w),
then edit it as needed — adjust the colors or add your logo according to your design requirements.

## 2. Design editing guidelines {#design-guidelines}

- You may freely change the **colors** to match your brand identity.
- **Logos, text and graphic elements** must stay **within the designated template area**.
- **Do not delete the guide layers** — hide them if they are not needed.

## 3. Sheet material {#material}

Print on **one** of the following materials.

- **Glossy** sheet sticker
- **Matte** sheet sticker

Refer to the photo below for the placement area.

# Charging

The RBQ10 can be charged using the supplied charger or docking station. The charger uses the charging port on the top of the robot; the docking station charges through the port on the bottom. You can also connect a charging cable to the docking station and then connect it to the charging port on the top of the robot to charge.

<div class="sb sb-warning">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">WARNING</p>
<p>Charge the robot only with the supplied RBQ10 charger or RBQ10 docking station.</p>
</div>
</div>

#### Step 1: Position the robot so the front or rear camera faces the docking station.

<p class="custom-block-title">REQUIRED READING</p>
<p>The distance between the docking station and the robot must be within 3 meters, and the front or rear camera must be able to recognize ArUco markers before automatic docking is possible.</p>
</div>
</div>

#### Step 2: Press the `Docking` button.

<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>When the robot recognizes a QR code, the docking sequence starts automatically.</p>
</div>
</div>

#### Step 3: The robot automatically attempts docking and, on failure, automatically retries.

  <img style="max-width: 100%; width: min(700px, 100%); height: auto; display: block; margin: 1rem auto; border-radius: 8px;" src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/charging/charging-6.png" alt="Charging via dock external cable step 3" />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ Charge robot with external cable ]</figcaption>
</figure>

## Docking station installation precautions

1. The charging station is water-resistant, but if water is present on the charging terminals, charging problems may occur; install it away from places where water splashes.
2. The power cable is treated for water exposure, but when connecting to an external outlet, keep water out of the plug connection.
3. Prolonged direct sunlight can cause overheating; installing in a shaded location is recommended.
4. Secure the charging station to the floor using the fixing holes.

# Controller and Wi-Fi

How to put the controller (Steam Deck, tablet, or PC) on the robot's Wi-Fi, connect the RBQ app to
the robot, and run the auto-start. Set the initial pose and power the robot on first — see
[Robot initial pose](./initial-pose).

## Step 1: Open the app

Launch the **RBQ** app on the controller. If it is not yet installed on a Steam Deck, start with
[Steam Deck setup](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/troubleshooting/steamdeck-setup.html). The installers are on
[Downloads](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/downloads/).

## Step 2: Join the robot's Wi-Fi {#wifi}

The robot provides a Wi-Fi access point named `RBQ_{XX}` (XX differs per unit). The controller must
be on that network to reach the robot.

The app opens on the **hub**. The robot name sits at the top left with the connection state right
after it, and that status line is what tells you whether the device is on the right network.

![The hub — robot name and status line](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/hub.pc.en.png)

1. **Read the status line** — `Connect to the robot's WiFi` means no robot is saved yet, and
   `Not on the robot's WiFi` means the device is on some other network. When the app knows the
   robot's WiFi it names it (*Robot WiFi(SSID) — please switch to it*).
2. **Switch networks** — on Linux desktop and Steam Deck the `Switch WiFi` button next to the line
   joins that network directly, or opens the in-app list so you can pick `RBQ_{XX}`; enter the
   password there if the network is secured. On Android, `WiFi settings` opens the system Wi-Fi
   screen instead.
3. **Confirm** — you are ready once the dot in front of the robot name turns green.

If `RBQ_{XX}` is not in the list, check that the robot is powered on and its Wi-Fi is up.

Once you reach the control home, the Wi-Fi chip in its top bar shows the signal strength. Tap it for
**My device WiFi**, which names the network your device is on and shows a `Robot network` (green) or
`Not robot network` (amber) badge.

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>Android policy forbids scanning from inside the app, so it offers only a <strong>System WiFi settings</strong> button. iOS and browser builds cannot read or change Wi-Fi either — join the network from the device's own Wi-Fi settings.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Step 3: Connect to the robot {#connect}

Robots are chosen and added on the hub. There is no connection screen inside Settings.

1. **Tap the robot name (▾)** to open **Select robot**. It lists the robots saved on this device
   and, while you are logged in, the robots assigned to your account.
2. **Tap the robot's row** to connect. On Linux desktop and Steam Deck the app switches to the
   robot's WiFi first when that network is saved and in range.
3. **For a robot you have not used before**, press `Add robot`. On the robot's own AP the app finds
   it by itself at the fixed address `192.168.0.10` — `Check again` retries. A robot behind a router
   or reachable at a public address is added under **Connect by address** (`Robot IP`, preset to
   `192.168.0.10`, or `Public IP`), and `Enter access code` registers the robots assigned to your
   account for remote (LTE) use.
4. **Communication is open** once the dot is green and the line reads `Connected` followed by the
   route.

![Select robot](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/hub-robots.pc.en.png)

The routes, the automatic connection at start-up and what each status line means are covered in
[Connection](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/gui/connection.html).

## Step 4: Auto-start {#auto-start}

This brings the robot software and state up in one go.

1. **Press auto-start** — before start-up, an `Auto Start` button sits on the hub under the robot
   status, and at the bottom center of the control home. (The hub card only appears once a robot is
   connected; the control-home pill is there before that, but grayed out.)

<figure style="text-align: center; margin: 0.5rem auto 1.25rem;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/boot-prestart.pc.en.png' alt='Auto start button on the pre-start home screen' style="display: block; width: 100%; max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 0 auto; border-radius: 6px; box-shadow: 0 1px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.07);" />
  <figcaption style="margin-top: 0.5rem; text-align: center; color: var(--vp-c-text-2, #666); font-size: 0.95em;">[ Home screen before start-up ]</figcaption>
</figure>

2. **Confirm** — a confirmation appears. Check that the robot is on flat ground with every foot and
   knee touching it, then press `Auto Start`. The row in the middle lists the stages ahead:
   `POWER`, `CAN-BUS`, `HOMING`, `IMU-CHECK`, `START`.

<figure style="text-align: center; margin: 0.5rem auto 1.25rem;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/boot-autostart-confirm.pc.en.png' alt='Auto-start confirmation' style="display: block; width: 100%; max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 0 auto; border-radius: 6px; box-shadow: 0 1px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.07);" />
  <figcaption style="margin-top: 0.5rem; text-align: center; color: var(--vp-c-text-2, #666); font-size: 0.95em;">[ Auto-start confirmation ]</figcaption>
</figure>

3. **Watch it run** — the same window turns into the **start-up sequence** and reports each stage as
   it completes, per leg and per joint with its elapsed time, so a failure points straight at the
   joint responsible.

<figure style="text-align: center; margin: 0.5rem auto 1.25rem;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/boot-autostart-running.pc.en.png' alt='Auto-start in progress' style="display: block; width: 100%; max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 0 auto; border-radius: 6px; box-shadow: 0 1px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.07);" />
  <figcaption style="margin-top: 0.5rem; text-align: center; color: var(--vp-c-text-2, #666); font-size: 0.95em;">[ Auto-start in progress ]</figcaption>
</figure>

4. **Confirm completion** — start-up is done once every item reads as complete and the robot is
   standing. Press the status in the top bar to review the individual results.

<figure style="text-align: center; margin: 0.5rem auto 1.25rem;">
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/app/home-status.pc.en.png' alt='Status popover after start-up' style="display: block; width: 100%; max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 0 auto; border-radius: 6px; box-shadow: 0 1px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.07);" />
  <figcaption style="margin-top: 0.5rem; text-align: center; color: var(--vp-c-text-2, #666); font-size: 0.95em;">[ Start-up complete — status ]</figcaption>
</figure>

<div class="sb sb-warning">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">WARNING</p>
<p>If auto-start does not finish, or an item is left failed, make sure nobody is nearby, review the <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/emergency-stop-procedures.html">emergency stop procedures</a>, and follow the steps below. Always observe the <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/general-safety-warning-precautions.html">general safety precautions</a> before operating.</p>
<ol style="margin: 0.5rem 0 0 1.25rem;">
<li>If the communication check failed: power the robot down safely and restart it.</li>
<li>If finding the home pose failed: check the leg posture on a flat, stable surface as described in <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/safety/maintenance-safety.html">maintenance safety</a>, then restart.</li>
</ol>
<p style="margin-top: 0.75rem;">If the problem persists, contact Rainbow Robotics as described on the <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/support/">Contact</a> page.</p>
</div>
</div>

SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/operation/emo.html

# Emergency Stop and Recovery Procedures

## Emergency stop using the button

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/emo.png' alt='Emergency stop button on rear of robot' />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ Emergency stop push button on the rear of the robot ]</figcaption>
</figure>

When the robot’s **emergency stop button** is pressed, all joints switch to **High Damping**. In this state, the robot’s legs resist external motion but **do not** accept torque or position commands.
This is a safety mode to protect the user and the robot in an emergency or unintended motion.

<div class="sb sb-note">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-note-i" aria-hidden="true">i</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">NOTE</p>
<p>During emergency stop, control is disabled and the robot may lose posture and settle to the ground under gravity.</p>
</div>
</div>

To recover from emergency stop:

1. Rotate the emergency stop button clockwise and return it to its original position.
2. Press the "Stance" button in the GUI, or perform [Robot Initial Pose Setting](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/operation/initial-pose.html).
3. Follow the initialization steps to return the robot to a ready state.

This reinitializes joint control and robot posture correctly.

================================================================================
SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/operation/initial-pose.html
================================================================================

# Robot Initial Pose Setting

Place the robot on a flat floor so that all feet and knees contact the ground. Refer to the robot posture in the image below.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/initial-pose-1.png' alt='Initial pose setup step 1' />
  <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ RBQ10 Initial Pose ]</figcaption>
</figure>

## Step 1. A flat surface is required.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/initial-pose-2.png' alt='Initial pose setup step 2' />
</figure>

## Step 2. Fully fold the knee joint.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/initial-pose-3.png' alt='Initial pose setup step 3' />
</figure>

## Step 3. Rotate the hip pitch and roll joints so that the “feet” and “knee” joints touch the ground. There are three ground points. (Body Bumper, Knee Joint, Foot)

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/initial-pose-4.png' alt='Initial pose setup step 4' />
</figure>

## Turn On the Robot {#power-on}

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/operation/power-button.png" alt="Power button" style="width: 300px;" />
</figure>

<p>- Press <strong>Power Button</strong> and check the red light on the button</p>
<p>- Check for <strong>double-beep sound</strong></p>

# Packing
The RBQ10 is primarily stored and transported using a Pelican case. The model of the Pelican case used is the 1730 Protector Case. Please refer to the images below and store the RBQ10 along with other items accordingly.


## Robot packing and unpacking
The Pelican case has two layers. The lower layer holds the charger, spare rubber feet, and LiDAR; the RBQ10 is placed on top of them.
<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-1.png' alt='Pelican case lower layer layout' />
</figure>

After arranging items in the lower layer, carry the robot as shown in the figure and place it in the case.

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>The robot must be carried by two people working together.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Before transporting the robot, remove any additional equipment attached to it and turn off the power.</p>
</div>
</div>

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-2.png' alt='Carrying robot into case' />
</figure>

After setting the RBQ10 on the floor, extend the legs as shown in the figure.

Two people should carry the robot, each holding one of the leg areas marked in red.

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-3.png' alt='Transport with legs extended' />
</figure>

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>Be careful not to let any foreign objects get into the knee joint rotation area, and ensure fingers do not get pinched!</p>
</div>
</div>

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-4.png' alt='Knee joint caution pose' />
</figure>

Place the robot in the Pelican 1730 case to match the case shape.

After the body is in the case, fold the legs in this order:

### Step 1: Fold the front legs’ knee joints fully
<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-5.png' alt='Front leg knee fold step 1' />
</figure>

### Step 2: Rotate the front legs’ hip pitch joints and place the legs into the case recesses

<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-6.png' alt='Front leg hip pitch rotation step 2' />
</figure>
<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-7.png' alt='Front leg placed in case step 2 (continued)' />
</figure>

### Step 3: Rotate the rear legs’ hip pitch joints so the legs go over the front thighs

### Step 4: Fully extend the rear shins
<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/packing/packing-8.png' alt='Rear leg shin extension step 4' />
</figure>

Place the remote controller in the side storage next to the robot. Remaining empty space can be used as needed.

Close the lid to finish packing.

Unpacking is the reverse of the above steps.

# Accessories

RBQ supports a range of optional accessories that extend the robot for field missions and
development work — sensing, onboard compute and connectivity, and power infrastructure.

## Sensing {#sensing}

<div class="rbq-card-grid">

  <div class="rbq-card">
    <img src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/ptz-camera.png" alt="" />
    <h3 id="ptz-camera">PTZ Camera<a class="header-anchor" href="#ptz-camera" aria-label="Permalink to PTZ Camera"></a></h3>
    <p>A Pan-Tilt-Zoom camera that mounts on the RBQ body. Provides high-resolution video streaming for surveillance and reconnaissance missions with remote pan, tilt, and zoom control via the GUI and API.</p>
    <a class="rbq-card-cta" href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/related-products/ptz-camera.html">Specifications →</a>
  </div>

  <div class="rbq-card">
    <img src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/accessories/mid-360.png" alt="" />
    <h3 id="lidar-mid-360">LIDAR (mid-360)<a class="header-anchor" href="#lidar-mid-360" aria-label="Permalink to LIDAR (mid-360)"></a></h3>
    <p>The Livox MID-360 is a compact 3D LiDAR with a hemispherical field of view (360° × 59°). Used for obstacle detection and autonomous navigation. Connects via Ethernet.</p>
    <p>The <strong>MID-360S</strong> is Livox's next-generation model: 360° horizontal by −7°–52° vertical, 40 m range at 10% reflectivity, 200,000 points per second. On the RBQ it is <strong>mounted rotated 90° about the vertical axis</strong>, so its frames differ from the MID-360 — see the <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/hardware/coordinate-frames.html#mid-360s">transform matrices</a>.</p>
    <a class="rbq-card-cta" href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/related-products/lidar.html#mid-360">Specifications →</a>
  </div>

  <div class="rbq-card">
    <img src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/accessories/ouster.png" alt="" />
    <h3 id="lidar-os1-32">LIDAR (OS1-32)<a class="header-anchor" href="#lidar-os1-32" aria-label="Permalink to LIDAR (OS1-32)"></a></h3>
    <p>The Ouster OS1-32 is a 360° spinning LiDAR with 32 channels that delivers dense point clouds for wide-area 3D mapping.</p>
    <a class="rbq-card-cta" href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/related-products/lidar.html#os1-32">Specifications →</a>
  </div>

</div>

## Compute &amp; Connectivity {#compute-connectivity}

<div class="rbq-card-grid">

  <div class="rbq-card">
    <img src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/accessories/user-pc-module.png" alt="" />
    <h3 id="user-pc-module">User-PC Module<a class="header-anchor" href="#user-pc-module" aria-label="Permalink to User-PC Module"></a></h3>
    <p>An embedded compute board that mounts inside the RBQ payload bay. Runs user applications, AI inference, and custom sensor processing directly on the robot. Offers multiple I/O interfaces for sensor integration.</p>
    <p>Available options:</p>
    <ul>
      <li><strong>UP Xtreme i12</strong> — Intel Core i7 (12th gen)</li>
      <li><strong>UP Xtreme i14</strong> — Intel Core i7 (14th gen)</li>
      <li><strong>NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin</strong> — for AI inference workloads</li>
    </ul>
    <p>For other PC configurations, please <a href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/support/">contact us</a>.</p>
    <a class="rbq-card-cta" href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/network.html#onboard-pcs-and-ip-addresses">Network &amp; IP →</a>
  </div>

  <div class="rbq-card">
    <img src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/accessories/hub-module.png" alt="" />
    <h3 id="hub-module">Hub Module<a class="header-anchor" href="#hub-module" aria-label="Permalink to Hub Module"></a></h3>
    <p>An interface hub that expands the number of usable <code>12V-LAN</code> ports, so more accessories can be connected at once. Simplifies wiring for multi-sensor payloads.</p>
    <a class="rbq-card-cta" href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/external-port.html">External ports →</a>
  </div>

  <div class="rbq-card">
    <img src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/accessories/wifi-module.png" alt="" />
    <h3 id="wifi-lte-gps-module">Wifi Module / LTE/GPS Module<a class="header-anchor" href="#wifi-lte-gps-module" aria-label="Permalink to Wifi Module / LTE/GPS Module"></a></h3>
    <p>Wireless communication modules for remote operation. The WiFi module enables high-bandwidth local communication, while the LTE/GPS module provides wide-area cellular connectivity combined with positioning.</p>
    <a class="rbq-card-cta" href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/network.html">Network →</a>
  </div>

</div>

## Payload Cabling {#payload-cabling}

Cables for wiring your own payload into the robot's power and communication. The robot end mates
directly with the MOCO waterproof connectors on the external port panel; the other end is wired to
suit your equipment. Voltage and current limits and the pin assignment for each port are in
[External ports](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/external-port.html#user-port-pin-map).

<div class="rbq-card-grid">

  <div class="rbq-card">
    <h3 id="cable-12pin">12PIN MOCO — 12V + LAN<a class="header-anchor" href="#cable-12pin" aria-label="Permalink to 12PIN MOCO — 12V + LAN"></a></h3>
    <p>Connects to the <code>12V/LAN</code> port on a version 2 panel and breaks out <strong>12 V power and Gigabit Ethernet</strong> in one run. For cameras and sensors that need both power and a network link.</p>
    <a class="rbq-card-cta" href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/external-port.html#lan-v2">Pin map →</a>
  </div>

  <div class="rbq-card">
    <h3 id="cable-4pin">4PIN MOCO — 48V + CAN<a class="header-anchor" href="#cable-4pin" aria-label="Permalink to 4PIN MOCO — 48V + CAN"></a></h3>
    <p>Connects to the <code>PWR-CAN</code> port (<code>PWR/CAN</code> on a version 2 panel) and breaks out <strong>battery power and the CAN bus</strong> together. For actuators and devices driven over CAN.</p>
    <a class="rbq-card-cta" href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/external-port.html#pwr-can">Pin map →</a>
  </div>

  <div class="rbq-card">
    <h3 id="cable-2pin">2PIN MOCO — 48V<a class="header-anchor" href="#cable-2pin" aria-label="Permalink to 2PIN MOCO — 48V"></a></h3>
    <p>Connects to the <code>POWER</code> port and carries <strong>battery power only</strong>. For loads that need no communication link.</p>
    <a class="rbq-card-cta" href="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/external-port.html#power">Pin map →</a>
  </div>

</div>

<div class="sb sb-caution">
<div class="sb-icon"><span class="sb-warn" aria-hidden="true">⚠</span></div>
<div class="sb-content">
<p class="custom-block-title">CAUTION</p>
<p>The two 48 V cables carry <strong>raw battery voltage</strong>, which moves between 42.0 V and 58.4 V with the state of charge. Add your own converter if the payload needs a regulated supply. Design within the per-port current limit — <code>POWER</code> 5 A, <code>PWR-CAN</code> 10 A, <code>12V/LAN</code> 2–3 A.</p>
</div>
</div>

How to mate and release the connectors is covered in [Connector handling](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/maintenance/connector.html);
switching power on to a port is covered in [Powering the external ports](https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/interface/port-power.html).

SOURCE: https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/manual/product-descriptions/general-specification.html

# RBQ Series

Rainbow Robotics' RBQ quadruped series is designed to be easy for anyone to use. Based on dynamics-based gait control and learning-based locomotion, it can move stably in unstructured environments such as rough terrain, slopes, and stairs. With various sensors, interfaces, and payload options, it can be used for field-oriented missions such as surveillance, reconnaissance, and safety management.

As a development platform, RBQ provides diverse interfaces, APIs, and SDKs so users can easily develop, integrate, and test their own robot applications.

* **Durability:** With an IP54 rating and a highly durable mechanical structure, RBQ can operate reliably in harsh environments for extended periods.
* **Expandability:** Built-in expansion network interfaces and power outputs support additional equipment and sensors. It also provides a developer-friendly software environment for rapid prototyping and integration.
* **Mobility:** RBQ can be transported in a dedicated case using a standard vehicle. It is designed for easy handling during transport, setup, and operation.

<figure>
    <img
    src="https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/RBQ_rendered.png" alt="RBQ quadruped robot" style="max-width: 100%; width: 480px; height: auto;"
    />
    <figcaption style="text-align: center;">[ RBQ 10 ]</figcaption>
</figure>

# Docking Station

The docking station helps RBQ automatically charge by moving to the charging station and executing a charging command when a mission is complete or the battery is low. With the docking station, the robot can repeatedly perform missions with minimal human intervention.
<figure>
  <img src='https://rainbowrobotics.github.io/RBQ/images/hardware/docking-station.png' alt='RBQ10 docking station' style="display: block; margin: 0 auto; width: 60%; height: auto;" />

Livox's next-generation 3D LiDAR. On the RBQ it is **mounted rotated 90° about the vertical axis**, so the connector faces robot-left on the front unit and robot-right on the rear one.
